utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody. We resume the hearing in the case Prosecutor versus Limaj, Bala, and Musliu. As scheduled, we'll have this morning the -- we'll start with the submissions by the Prosecution, in the appeals of the Prosecution. I take note that it was mentioned yesterday the Defence of Mr. Limaj has filed a document containing answers to questions posed by the Appeals Chamber. I don't know whether it has been filed already or will be filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: It will be filed. Thank you. I take note of that. I will not repeat the times in the Scheduling Order. This is well-known by the parties. Of course it's -- goes without saying that what I said yesterday, that parties should not repeat what's in the brief as much as possible, is very much appreciated by the Appeals Chamber. And of course, if this brings to shorten the hearing, that will be also welcome. So I give the floor to the Prosecutor for its submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning, Your Honours. I'll be addressing Your Honours this morning on the Prosecution's appeal against both Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu, specifically grounds 1 and 2 of the Prosecution appeal against both respondents. After that, Mr. Wirth will address you on ground 3, relating to JCE, which applies to all three respondents in this case. And finally, Ms. Margetts will address on the Prosecution's appeal against the sentence of Mr. Bala. The Prosecution is appealing the acquittals rendered by the Trial Chamber against both Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu because the Trial Chamber's findings were ones no reasonable trier of fact could have made. The Trial Chamber made these findings largely because it misapplied the standard of proof, and as a result a miscarriage of justice has occurred. Two men, who on the evidence should have been convicted, were acquitted. As this Appeals Chamber has observed in the Stakic appeals judgement, when the Prosecution appeals against factual findings against it, it bears a heavy burden of persuasion. It's not enough in this appeal for us to persuade you that their guilt was a reasonable inference available on the evidence. We must persuade you that this is the only reasonable conclusion, that the evidence cannot reasonably be seen as consistent with a finding other than guilt. That's a significant burden, but one that the Prosecution can meet in this case. The only reasonable conclusion which can be drawn from all of the evidence is that from late May until the 26th of July, 1998, Fatmir Limaj was in overall command of the area of Lapusnik in which the prison was located and was actively present in the prison. And in that same time-period Isak Musliu was also present in the prison, at times beating and mistreating detainees and had effective command over the prison and the KLA soldiers in it. Before I turn to each of the Prosecution appeals individually against Mr. Limaj and Mr. Musliu, I want to start by saying a few words on the nature of the errors in this case and the remedy which is available if this Chamber does find, in the case of one or both, that the Trial Chamber erred in law or in fact. Our appeals against Mr. Limaj and Mr. Musliu are not simply appeals based on errors of fact, as the respondents have claimed. For both of them, the Trial Chamber legally erred through its erroneous application of the standard of proof. Let me be more specific. In our submission, the Trial Chamber first applied a standard of proof that was not based on reasonable doubt, but rather one that entertained any doubt, including that not based on the evidence and, at times, even contrary to logic and common sense. Secondly, it applied this standard -- it applied this standard to individual pieces of evidence rather than reserving its application, as it should have done, to the elements of the crimes and the facts indispensable for entering a conviction. Since the standard of proof is the lens through which the fact-finder must assess the evidence, in our submission their legal error has coloured and given rise to many of the Trial Chamber's factual findings, which amounted to errors of fact. And then in addition, the Trial Chamber made errors of fact on many other findings. If this Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber did legally err in applying the standard of proof, which invalidated the decision, then in accordance with or in line with the standards of review set out by this Chamber in the cases of Blaskic and Kordic, particularly Kordic paragraphs 24, subparagraph B, this Chamber should then apply the correct legal standard to the evidence and decide if you are convinced beyond reasonable doubt as to the guilt of the respondents. We've set this out more thoroughly in our appeal brief, particularly paragraph 2.291 and in our reply brief, paragraphs 1.7 to 1.15. We would also say that because the effect of the legal error in this case is so far-reaching on the factual findings, this is one of those cases where it would be necessary for this Chamber to review all of the evidence; and having done so, in our submission, you will be satisfied that guilt is the only reasonable conclusion, uphold our appeal, and convict the respondents. In the alternative, if the Chamber is not -- does not find that the Trial Chamber legally erred but does find that it's factually erred and has caused the miscarriage of justice, the Chamber can enter either new convictions, such as the Chamber did in Tadic, the Tadic case, or the Krnojelac case, or you could quash the findings and the verdicts and remit the case to a new Trial Chamber for a new trial. I'll turn now to the Prosecution's appeal against Fatmir Limaj. The Trial Chamber believed that there was a reasonable possibility that Fatmir Limaj was not the man that witnesses said they met in the camp, the one they referred to as the commander or Commander Celiku. And further, that there was a reasonable possibility that at the relevant time he was not in overall command of the area of Lapusnik in which the prison was located. These are the findings in paragraphs 565 and 601 of the judgement. On the evidence, neither possibility was reasonable and they came about because of the Trial Chamber's misapplication of the standard of proof. Now, the Defence, in its response brief, has pointed out that the Trial Chamber did correctly articulate in several paragraphs of the trial judgement, for example, paragraphs 10, 20, 561, 601, the standard of proof and its approach to the evidence. And we acknowledge these -- these exist in the judgement. Our point is that a proper review of the trial judgement, and in particular the Trial Chamber's forensic approach to the evidence, does not bear out that the Trial Chamber applied this standard and this approach in relation to the facts needed to convict Mr. Limaj. And I'll turn first to the Trial Chamber's finding about his command. This is the finding in 601 and it's ground 2 of our appeal against Mr. Limaj. Now, Mr. Limaj didn't dispute that he was in charge of the Celiku 1 unit based in Klecka from April 1998 or that the 121 Brigade was officially formed in August/September, the fall of 1998, with him as the brigade commander. And he didn't dispute that its area of responsibility, the 121 Brigade, included that part of Lapusnik lying south of the Peje-Prishtine road. But what he did dispute - and this became the critical issue for the Trial Chamber - was whether the command situation in autumn 1998 was, in fact, in place earlier at the time of the events relevant to the indictment. The only reasonable conclusion that can be drawn from all the evidence is that the organisation of the 121 Brigade merely formalised the situation which had been in fact in the months preceding, that is, from late May until late July, that he commanded a region extending beyond Klecka, including the part of Lapusnik lying below the road where the prison was located. And it was not reasonably possible, as the Trial Chamber found, that his responsibility did not extend in this way. The Defence has claimed in their responses, that what we're trying to do is to relitigate this issue and they argue that it's clear from paragraphs 601 to 602 that the Trial Chamber did review all this evidence. Our full argument is contained in the appeal brief, paragraphs 2.129 to 2.228. Today I merely wish to highlight some matters which demonstrate both this legally flawed approach by the Trial Chamber and the unreasonableness of its finding. I should emphasise at the outset, we take no issue with the Trial Chamber individually assessing the various pieces of evidence one by one, but the problem arises when, as here, the trier of fact then fails to properly consider the cumulative effect of all of these individual pieces of evidence together. In essence, what the Trial Chamber did was to assess and to knock out each piece of evidence individually on the basis that it was itself insufficient to prove the issue, then leaving it with nothing to consider in the final analysis or the final mix when coming to consider whether an essential fact was proved. And here we're talking about the fact of his command. So as a result of this approach, it failed to properly consider the interlocking nature and the corroborative -- the corroboration among the various witnesses and documents, and this can be seen, this is especially apparent in its approach to three KLA military offices: Ramiz Qeriqi, also known as Luan; Shukri Buja; and Ramadan Behluli, all of whom have said that Fatmir Limaj from his base in Klecka was the senior regional commander in the area at the time to whom each was either directly or indirectly subordinated. Now, I'll elaborate a little bit more on this. Ramiz Qeriqi, then deputy commander in Kroimire and under Shukri Buja's command, testified that Mr. Limaj's authority extended to a much wider area than Klecka and, in fact, included Lapusnik. I'm now going to -- I'm now going to show a portion of his testimony. I want to play some of his testimony where he testifies this -- about this line of command that went from the General Staff in Likovc, with Rexhep Selimi in command, to the regional level of Klecka with Limaj in command and then to his unit which was in Kroimire. And this is transcript T3579, lines 3 to 20. It's on your screens, Your Honours, I think it should be coming through now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: "Q. Mr. Qeriqi, at this time, where was the command that was just above you and Shukri Buja? Where was it based? "A. I think Shukri knows better. I said I came from Likovc to Klecke and from Klecke to Kroimire and this is how the organisation line was. "Q. The organisation went from Likovc to Klecka to Kroimire. "A. Yes. "Q. And who was the commander in Klecka? "A. I think you must have forgotten. I said earlier that Fatmir was the commander in Klecke. In Likovc, it was Rexhep Selimi. The general commander was Azem Syla. I think I already stated this earlier."

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Later in his testimony this witness mentioned that the area was the same when he was a battalion commander, and we know that he did not become a battalion commander until August of 1998, but due to the Trial Chamber's own misunderstanding of the evidence, it thought that the witness may have been uncertain about the areas of responsibility in the two respective time-periods or confused about the period under discussion, that's in paragraph 573. We've set out this in detail in our brief at paragraph 2.202. The clear import of the testimony of this witness was that the area of responsibility was the same, both before and after the formal establishment of the brigades and the battalions. Compounding this, the Trial Chamber then failed to consider that Shukri Buja and Ramadan Behluli closely corroborated that witness's evidence. Again, we've set out this in detail in our briefs so I can be quite short in my submissions today on this point. But, in essence, it's this: In their 2003 interviews with the Office of the Prosecution, Shukri Buja and Ramadan Behluli each said and each drew maps or diagrams to the same effect, confirming that Limaj from his base in Klecka was at the time the regional commander of a number of units in the region, including those in the Lapusnik, area of Lapusnik, below the road. And I invite Your Honours to review these interviews carefully. Mr. Buja's interview, P160.1 and Mr. Behluli's, P121. What is especially compelling is the fact that four witnesses, Witness Qeriqi, Witness Behluli, Witness Buja, and L-64 independently drew strikingly similar diagrams of this organisational structure or outlined maps of the area of command in the same way. And I'll show now on your screens what I mean by this. The first is Mr. -- Witness Qeriqi's map, which is P154, it's a black-and-white image, but in the left-hand side of your screens you'll see the encircled area which this witness said was under Limaj's command at the time and includes the area of Lapusnik. That's the time-period May/June 1998, and it's at transcript page 3580 to 81. Now, after you've considered that, I'll show now on the screen Witness Behluli's map, P119, and you'll see the remarkable consistency there between the maps, the same area being circled showing the area of command under Limaj during this time-period and including Lapusnik. This one's highlighted in yellow so it's a little bit more easy to see. Finally, I'll show you Mr. Buja's drawing of the organisational structure, which is P159, and basically this shows the Klecka, the unit -- the Klecka command in the centre point of that diagram, and spinning out from that are the various units that Mr. Buja in his OTP interview said were commanded under Limaj during the time-period, and some of the writing is not so easy to read, but at the bottom of the screen you'll see the reference to Lapusnik and Kroimire and the various other units as they continue in that bottom part of the diagram. Now, we know that when Mr. Buja and Mr. Behluli came to court, they recanted their earlier statements. Basically these witnesses air-brushed out Klecka, they air-brushed out Limaj as the intermediary level of authority and claimed that their earlier statements had related to the situation pertaining after August. And as we also know, these two witnesses were declared hostile and their prior interviews were admitted into evidence as substantive evidence. Their in-court testimony was nothing but a tissue of lies. The Trial Chamber itself observed that their testimony in court was due to a clear desire not to give any evidence which could incriminate Limaj and out of an evident sense of bondship with the KLA and Fatmir Limaj. In fact, when they admitted -- when the Trial Chamber admitted the earlier interviews into evidence in their decision of the 25th of April, 2005, in relation to Behluli, the Trial Chamber said that he demonstrated an unpreparedness to tell the truth. In our submission, the Trial Chamber made a critical error by not giving any weight to the evidence in their earlier interviews, even though they acknowledged these interviews were freely given and even though the contents of their interviews were corroborated in material parts. In essence, the Trial Chamber rewarded these two witnesses for their conscious efforts to mislead the Trial Chamber in what can only be described as a transparent effort to protect Fatmir Limaj by concluding that their consciously untruthful court testimony rendered void their eminently more reliable evidence in their prior interviews. That's in paragraphs 581 and 586. Now, we acknowledge that the Trial Chamber cited additional reasons for rejecting their earlier interviews, for example, set out at Trial Chamber 582, but if -- but a review of the whole of Buja and Behluli's interviews reveals that these concerns were simply unfounded. Firstly, it contrasts with the view of the Trial Chamber itself during the trial, for example, saying Buja's interview was fair and the questions were clear. And in relation to Behluli, given the numerous references in that interview to the time-period being discussed in that interview, and even the fact that Behluli himself mentions various events in the time-period to show that he was clearly aware of what time-period was being discussed in that interview, it is hard to discern that they could have been confused about the time-period under discussion. And in relation to Witness Behluli, his single reference to Luan as being a battalion commander cannot be a reason to exclude the whole interview. The Trial Chamber's legally flawed approach also meant that it did not properly consider or treat as corroborating an array of other evidence, and we've set this all out in our brief, and I'll only mention some of the most salient points. First, his official appointment as brigade commander of the 121 Brigade in August 1998, and then later followed in November 1998 by his appointment to the KLA General Staff. Is it really believable that by August 1998 Fatmir Limaj was determined to be the most qualified person to command the 121 Brigade, encompassing all the units in the region, and yet in the immediately preceding period he was merely in charge of one unit of some 20 -- 10 to 20 men in Klecka, a protected village not on the front line? In our submission, it could not be. Limaj also played other roles at this time which are similarly discordant with his account and consistent with the Prosecution's position. On your screens now you'll see a still image from a television footage of the first KLA public address, an important occasion on the 14th of June, 1998. This is from Exhibit P034. And on your screens you'll see there, on the right of your screens, there's Mr. Limaj flanking the KLA spokesperson Jakup Krasniqi, as he makes this important address. I also mention Limaj's role in a KLA oath ceremony in Lapusnik in late June/early July and his accompanying General Staff -- senior General Staff to inspect the placement of a mortar along the Peje-Prishtine road in the Lapusnik gorge. There's also the evidence of his disarming soldiers in other units, such as Fadil Kastrati and L-64. And in addition, his attendance on the 30th of July, just a couple of days, a few days after the fall of Lapusnik, at the high-level meeting which was held with EU representatives in Klecka at which the Austrian representative there, Mr. Kickert, recorded him as being: "The regional Commander Celiku." There's also the evidence of Sylejman Selimi. He was the KLA commander of the Drenica Zone, the zone above, the zone which Limaj was in, who said that the boundary of his zone only went as far south as the Peje-Pristina road, and that's at transcript 2088 and 2149. And the last piece of evidence I'll mention is Exhibit P34, the image came from P34. This is the KLA documentary in -- which was made in 2002, that is, before the indictments were issued. It's a documentary which commemorates a fallen KLA fighter, and in those interviews -- in interviews in that documentary, Limaj and other KLA soldiers freely recount the early days of the KLA and they recount a very telling, a very clear message. You have to watch the whole of the documentary in order to understand, to glean the message. And the one clear message was this: That the units which formally became the 121 Brigade in August/September of 1998 were, in fact, operational and functioning under Limaj in the period immediately before then. The Defence in response criticised us for not addressing the Defence witnesses put forward on their behalf such as Rexhep Selimi and Bislim Zyrapi, who were also considered by the Trial Chamber, and we've set this out -- we've replied in detail in our reply, paragraph 2.46 to 2.63. The main point is that the Trial Chamber essentially accepted their evidence without the same critique of their reliability and credibility as they reserved for Prosecution witnesses. Simply put, the finding as to Mr. Limaj's command was not one a reasonable Trial Chamber could have reached upon a proper evaluation of the evidence and applying the standard of proof to the whole of the evidence. I'll turn now to the Trial Chamber's other unreasonable finding in relation to Fatmir Limaj, and this was the reasonable possibility that Fatmir Limaj was not the person several detainees said they met in the camp and referred to as Commander Celiku or the commander. Four independent, yet interlocking, strands of evidence: Visual identification, pseudonym, command position, and proximity lead to the inescapable conclusion that it was him. And the Trial Chamber failed to reach the only reasonable conclusion because it did not properly draw these strands of evidence together. I'll be very brief on command in this part because I've already developed this point in my submissions. The main point about the command evidence is that the Trial Chamber should not have artificially dissected it from the identification evidence. The evidence that Mr. Limaj was at least a commander in the region should have been the lens for looking at the evidence of the detainees who said he was the "Commander Celiku" or the commander from the prison who was involved with their release. Now, as for proximity, the point about proximity, we don't suggest, of course, that his frequent presence in Lapusnik and his proximity to the prison proves that he was the man detainees met in the prison. By itself, it's not conclusive. We accept that. But it is very relevant. And to make this point, I'd like to show now two images, the first one Exhibit 001, image 8, which is on your screens now. So we can see the relative size of Lapusnik. This is an aerial photograph of the part of Lapusnik which lies south of the Peje-Pristina road. And the prison compound is the one marked with the red circle around it. The road -- the Peje-Prishtine road is the large asphalt road which runs on the top of that photograph. And Limaj -- I note in this regard that Limaj agreed that he was actually in Lapusnik some 20 times in June and July 1998. And on our calculations, that amounts to something like two times per week. I'll also show you a second photograph which is Exhibit P006, because it's important to understand the physical construct of the prison compound and its surrounds. The Trial Chamber found that some 30 prisoners were detained here in this prison compound during a six-week period in June and July 1998. And I'll just point out some structures on this photograph to orientate Your Honours. You'll see building marked 1 on the left-hand, bottom left-hand side of your screens, that's the cow-shed, and immediately next to it is the storage room in which detainees were kept. Building number -- marked number 2 in the middle of the photograph is the main house in the prison -- it's the main house. And building marked number 3, which is on the right-hand side of that photograph as you look at it on your screens, is the prison compound, the Vojvoda -- excuse me, let me start again. The house marked number 3 that you see on the screens, next door to the prison compound, is the Vojvoda compound, where Limaj agreed that he attended a KLA oath ceremony. And I ask Your Honours to bear in mind the location of this compound, just metres from the camp, and the fact that Limaj attended this ceremony, the KLA oath ceremony, at the time while the camp was in operation in June or July 1998. I should also mention while we're on the topic of proximity that Limaj was in Lapusnik for significant battles in May and in July; that he went on one occasion with senior KLA General Staff to inspect a weapon placement near the Sopi compound, and this was the compound in which the Celiku 3 headquarters was located, and this was 200 metres from the prison; he also attended the clinic at this Sopi compound 200 metres from the prison. The Trial Chamber, in our submission, did not give due weight to these facts. The Defence has claimed that the argument that we're making about proximity or the relevance of proximity is inconsistent with our pre-trial brief, and in the pre-trial brief we said that the prison compound was guarded and out of view to those on the front line or in the village. In our submission, in light of the frequency and the nature of Fatmir Limaj's visits to Lapusnik, as at least a senior person in the region, at times metres from the prison as I've shown you, there's no inconsistency between our position today, or in this appeal, and the pre-trial brief. I'll come now to identification. There is one inescapable fact. Six witnesses, all found to be honest and credible, testified that while detained in the prison they met a man who they either recognised at the time was Commander Celiku, that's L-07; or subsequently recognised on television as the commander, that's Ivan Bakrac and Vojko Bakrac; or Commander Celiku, that's L-04; or - they described him invariably in different ways - or the one who ordered their release and that's L-06 and L-10. In other words, they saw his image on the television, determined it was him, believed it was him, and at that point that's when they learned his real name. All six picked Limaj as that person. I stress again, one recognised him at the time; five later saw his image on television and believed it was the man they'd met in the prison. These witnesses give very similar accounts of his appearance, and their descriptions of what he actually did in their encounters with him coincide with his actual rank as a commander. In these circumstances, was it reasonable for the Trial Chamber to consider what it called a - and I quote from the judgement - they called it a "clearly recognisable risk" that a number of witnesses may have been unconsciously influenced by subsequent media images of him. In other words, that rather than triggering the memory of these six people when they saw the image on TV, that the TV image actually created the memory, the same memory, in these six people. In our submission, the answer to that is no. I want to go now to look at Witness L-07's evidence. It was given in closed session, so for this part of the hearing I would like to close the hearing while we go in and listen to the transcript at T793, lines 25 to T794, line 25.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It's hard to compete with the noise of the shutters. The Trial Chamber found L-07's evidence was insufficiently reliable to identify Limaj as the person he met, and one reason for doing so was this spectre of unconscious transfer. In addition, L-07's evidence was corroborated and the Trial Chamber failed to properly consider this fact, and I can be very brief on these points because we have amply covered them in our appeal brief. Firstly, after his release from the prison, Ivan Bakrac recognised the person he called the commander that he met twice in the prison on two images: First on a TV broadcast of a funeral march on the 16th of June, 1998, in which Limaj was in or is in, that's P81; and then later in an image that he saw on the internet of Limaj, and that's P80. And it was then that he learnt his real name. The Trial Chamber erred, in our submission, in placing any significance on the fact that Ivan Bakrac failed to pick a clean-shaven photograph of Fatmir Limaj shown to him some four to five -- four years later, when his evidence had been of meeting a man who in his words were not freshly shaven. I think we've amply covered this in our appeal brief, paragraphs 2.102 to 6; in reply, paragraphs 2.17, so I won't repeat that except to note that the difficulties of recognising somebody when a person sees them with a beard and later sees them without the beard -- a beard, or sees photographs without a beard, are well-known. Mr. Wagenaar spoke about this in his evidence at transcript 7189 to 7197. The Trial Chamber also erred by rejecting the corroborative value that came through Vojko Bakrac's evidence, and specifically, I'm talking about the ICTY statement that he gave in 2005, this was after he testified, and in this statement he stated -- it was appending a statement he'd given to Serbian authorities in July of 1998, close to the time of his release from the prison, and in this ICTY statement which was admitted by the agreement of the parties, he said that having reviewed the statement that he gave to the Serb authorities in 1998 that it was accurate, and in paragraph 9 he says that he could remember now the events described in that statement. And the events that he described in the statement were essentially this, that while he was detained in the main house of the prison, Vojko Bakrac watched TV or was watching TV and he saw an image showing a convoy of men, and on that convoy image he recognised the commander that he had met in the prison at the front of that convoy. And I invite Your Honours to review P202 which was admitted in evidence, transcript page 5185 to 86. And the error stemmed from the fact that the Trial Chamber seemingly rejected it on the basis of its form, that it hadn't been -- this evidence had not been given live. Apart from Ivan and Vojko Bakrac we also have the evidence of L-04, 10, and 06. L-04 testified that the guard known to him as Tamuli told him that he would be taken to see Commander Celiku and then he met him. L-04 first learned his name from the television, his real name, from the television. L-10 said that a man came twice and asked why he was there, why he was being detained. And L-10 heard the guard Shala say his name was Celiku and he also learnt his real name from the television. Likewise, L-06 recognised the person who organised his release from the prison on television and learnt his name at that point. Now, the Trial Chamber may well have had difficulties in relying on any single one of these, but in our submission it was error not to have properly considered their cumulative effect. And the Trial Chamber's even partial reliance on this phenomenon of unconscious transfer to explain how six people chose Fatmir Limaj as that individual, as the person they met, that reliance was misplaced. As not -- it's simply not applicable. The witnesses recognised Fatmir Limaj as the person from the camp, from the prison, upon seeing him on the television spontaneously. It would be as if they were walking down the street and saw him and recognised him. Now, while we can see that there -- there could be an impact that a media exposure could have on a subsequent identification, we know this from DM003, paragraph 11, Mr. Wagenaar's report, but here - and leaving aside the courtroom identifications which had no probative value, in our submission - here there were none. It wasn't a case where they made later subsequent identifications from the photo-board and picked Mr. Limaj. And -- nor did the evidence establish that the TV images from which the witnesses recognised that man from the camp, they did not suggest that Limaj had somehow been involved in the Lapusnik prison or the crimes. And we can see this from the images that were circulating at that time, P80, P81, and even the 14th of June, 1998, image that I showed to Your Honours on the screen a moment ago. And this is even the case for the witnesses L-04, 06, and 12, who indicated that they saw him on television after the war. This is an example, in our submission, of the Trial Chamber relying on any doubt, not even doubt which was based on evidence, and common sense and logic. Finally, Your Honours, there's the striking evidence regarding his pseudonym. Three detainees testified that they heard other KLA soldiers, guards in the prison, refer to the man they met as Celiku or Commander Celiku. Two even said that when they were released on the Berisa Mountains they got their release papers under the orders of Commander Celiku. By focusing on the visual identification evidence, the Trial Chamber did not -- failed to properly consider the relevance of this pseudonym. Now, we acknowledge that the Trial Chamber did mention his pseudonym in other parts of the judgement, specifically the findings on command, but not here in this identification part, not here where it's doing this analysis. And this is another illustration, in our submission, of the Trial Chamber not applying the standard of proof to all evidence relevant to the fact. Numerous KLA soldiers, both Prosecution and Defence witnesses, confirmed that at the time, we're talking the spring and summer of 1998, they knew Fatmir Limaj as Celiku or Commander Celiku. Some even confirmed, such as Sylejman Selimi, Ramiz Qeriqi, some even confirmed that he was known as that name, Celiku or Commander Celiku, from March of 1998 when they first had dealings with him. And even Fatmir Limaj, who denied being personally known as Celiku until later, saying that this name was only reserved for the unit, his unit was called Celiku, even he conceded when confronted with -- on cross-examination with an interview he gave to an Albanian television on the 3rd of June, this was an -- this was -- this was introduced as "an interview with a Mr. Celiku, one of the KLA commanders." Even he had to concede in cross-examination that this name was circulating for him at that time. Critically there was no evidence before the Court that there was any other man operating in the area with that name. Even accepting the individual weaknesses of the six identification witnesses, the Trial Chamber erred by not finding that the combination of evidence, not just from the witnesses, but the combination of all the evidence eliminated the possibility that these six people were making an honest mistake. And I emphasise for this point, the Trial Chamber found all six to be honest and credible. The Trial Chamber made no findings that these witnesses lied in their evidence or somehow colluded in their evidence. Now, we acknowledge that the Trial Chamber in its judgement, paragraph 561, did state that it had considered the combined effect of the several identifications to determine whether they, in combination, displaced the risks of mistake in the individual identifications. But it concluded that the difficulties with respect to each of the identifications were, in the Trial Chamber's view, of such significance that "notwithstanding the strong possibility apparent on the evidence, it is, on final analysis, not able to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt that Fatmir Limaj is identified to be the person referred to in their evidence by the witnesses or any of them." This is in stark contrast with what we submit was the Trial Chamber's correct approach when it came to Mr. Bala, the correct approach in paragraph 631, where the Trial Chamber took the view that while no one of the identifications individually would have been sufficient, the combination overcame the individual deficits. And in our submission, it was due -- it was because of the Trial Chamber's own slicing or parsing, dissecting of evidence that it did not consider the whole of the evidence to see if it overcame the possibility that six separate people simply made an honest mistake. And by this I stress I'm not only referring to the fact that six people at various times and in various places chose him or picked him as that person. But all the evidence, for example, their hearing the pseudonym being used by the guards in the prison prior to meeting him, and his prison -- his proximity to the prison, and his position as commander at the time. The Trial Chamber is entitled to make individual assessments about the credibility and reliability on individual pieces of evidence. We take no issue with that. That is their function. But it is not entitled, as it did in paragraphs 531 to 565, to apply the standard to each piece of evidence. Drawing these strands together, there is no other reasonable conclusion; Fatmir Limaj was that person that witnesses met in the prison. We ask you to uphold both grounds 1 and 2 of the Prosecution's appeal against Fatmir Limaj. I do -- I will turn to Isak Musliu's -- our appeal against Isak Musliu, but if Your Honours have questions relating to Mr. Limaj, our appeal against Mr. Limaj, that might be a convenient point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, you were discussing Mr. Celiku's identity, and I think you said that there was no evidence that anybody else in the area carried that name. Well, did Prosecution lead any evidence that there was no one else in the area with that name?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution did not lead evidence to that effect; however, our submission would be or is that the overwhelming effect of all of the evidence of the Prosecution is that Fatmir Limaj was that person, Commander Celiku, and there's -- there's a count which both he and Rexhep Selimi give as to how the name -- of the etymology of that name and how it came about by the use of radios and the creation of Celiku 1 and Celiku 2 units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you another question. I was intrigued by your reference to the concept of unconscious transfer of images. Was there any necessity for technical evidence to be given on the subject; if so, was there any technical evidence on the subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: There was -- the only evidence about this came from Professor Wagenaar, so to that extent there was technical evidence on the subject. This is also a matter of -- that one could say is a matter of common knowledge. One can understand how unconscious transfer could occur, and I think Mr. Wagenaar's evidence brings out -- he details how that phenomenon can occur, even subtly, where a person doesn't recognise that he is being unconsciously affected by images. But of course our submission is that it has no place here because, of course, the first -- when the witnesses saw the image on television, that's where they recognised him. It's not a case -- unconscious transfer would be applicable if later the identification that we would rely on, if that identification was done after they had been exposed to those TV images.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, you were kind enough to refer to paragraph 561 in the trial court judgement with regard to the combined effect of the several identifications. Given our high deference for trial courts, are you asking us to disregard this statement in paragraph 561, that the Chamber did consider the combined effect of these identifications? What are we to make out of it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I think our point about paragraph 561 is slightly -- is somewhat different. We're not asking you to go behind the Trial Chamber. We can accept that they did consider the combined effect of the six identification witnesses, and you can see they're struggling. It's a very fine balance and at the end of the day they say there's a strong possibility but they're not convinced beyond reasonable doubt. Our point is that because of this parsing of the evidence, what the Trial Chamber should have done here is in addition to the consideration of the combination of the six witnesses, it ought -- it should also have considered the other evidence, for example, the pseudonym, the proximity, the commander position. There's nothing of that here, so this, in our submission, shows quite starkly the legal error in the Trial Chamber's approach to the evaluation of the evidence. They are only here considering whether the combination of visual identification can overcome the possibility for honest mistake. They are not considering other parts of the evidence, which should have been factored into that analysis if they were to apply the standard of proof in the correct fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Do I understand you correctly in that you wanted to convince us that at para 561 the Chamber, as a kind of lip-service, spoke about the combined effect, took this into consideration; however, gave no reason at all why these six witness testimonies taken together and the other factors you mentioned, that they -- that a reason should have been given why this combined effect does not suffice, that it amounts only to a strong possibility and, yeah, just to say the final analysis is not able to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, does not suffice, legally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think you put our position very well. There is no reasoning. Our first position is there is no reasoning. This is a lip-service to consideration of the combination of evidence without any reasoning apparent as to why the combination could not overcome the risk of honest mistake. That is the first point. The second one is, as well, that they haven't factored in the other parts of the evidence which they ought to have. It's all very well to consider these six, but in our submission there was more to it than just six people making an identification from television images or recognising him at the time in the case of L-07.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: But on this very point can you comment upon paragraph 562, where the Chamber in detail is giving reasoning?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Yes. We've addressed this quite thoroughly as well in our briefs. Here the Trial Chamber says, Well, we have considered the combined effect and we actually think that this highlights uncertainties or inconsistencies relating to their identifications. In our submission, and it's easier to set this out in our brief, the differences that the Trial Chamber noted were oftentimes it's own creation, if I can put it that way, they call these differences "arresting". If you look at the evidence, the clear import of the evidence of the witnesses is how strikingly similar these identifications are. They all give a very similar description of the appearance and the rank of Fatmir Limaj. So as a result of having made -- some of them were due to their own errors of fact, for example; differences in the size of the beard, whether it was a medium-sized beard, whether it was a closely trimmed beard. Many of these so-called differences among the witnesses were really more apparent than real, and the Trial Chamber was wrong to be concerned about these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Vaz.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You said earlier that Celiku, this name Celiku, was mainly a word dealing with units that were under the command of Commander Limaj. If this is what you said, could you please give us some specifications in this regard and tell us why this word "Celiku" would refer to Limaj. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: According to the evidence of Rexhep Selimi and the evidence of Fatmir Limaj, the derivation of the name came when Selimi gave two radios, one of whom went to Fatmir Limaj, and named one radio Celiku -- one radio was for the Celiku 1 unit and one radio was for the Celiku 2 unit. However, it has to be noted that many witnesses from as early as March, when they first meet Fatmir Limaj, they know him as Celiku or Commander Celiku. Now, the meaning of "Celiku" in Albanian is steel. Now, I can't assist Your Honour in telling you how this name may have been associated to Fatmir Limaj as the name "Steel". But it's clear that the names of the units derived from him, that he was Celiku -- he was Celiku, he was Commander Celiku, and the units under him were the Celiku units. I hope that answers Your Honour's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAZ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I believe there are no other questions. You may proceed, Ms. Brady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now then turn to the Prosecution's appeal against Isak Musliu. Our appeal brief sets out in detail how the Trial Chamber misapplied the standard of proof and made unreasonable findings, both as to his presence in the prison as the guard Qerqiz who beat detainees and regard his guard over the prison and the KLA guards working there. I'll begin with his presence in the prison. In short, the Trial Chamber's emphasis on visual identification meant that it did not properly consider other relevant and probative evidence regarding his participation. The only reasonable conclusion from all the evidence was that Isak Musliu was the person who three detainees referred to as Qerqiz, the masked man who beat them in the prison; the same person who two of his soldiers saw either in the prison, that's Witness Karpuzi, or entering and leaving it, that's Witness L-64, and who another detainee saw unmasked in the prison, and that's L-96. Notwithstanding that six witnesses identified this accused, either by his name because they knew him or his pseudonym, the Trial Chamber thought that it was a reasonable possibility it was not him. That was not reasonable; it actually defies common sense. And again, the Trial Chamber artificially separated the strands of evidence rather than drawing them together in a logical, cohesive manner. So, for example, when considering the evidence which directly placed Isak Musliu in the prison, it did not properly consider several other key facts, such as his command, he commanded Celiku 3, the sole armed force south of the road whose fighting positions were some 300 to 500 metres from the compound; as well as his regular presence and infrequent [sic] proximity to the prison throughout the months of May, June, and July. I'll put back on the screen Exhibit P006, this is the photo we've seen before of the prison compound and its surrounds. It doesn't have a number, but the building I want to focus on is behind the main house which is the building marked number 2, the main house is number 2, and behind that is a cluster of houses on the other side of what is a dirt road, and that is Gzim Gashi's compound. And this is where, during the relevant time, from the 29th of May, Celiku's three soldiers ate their meals and some even slept there on occasion. Now, Isak Musliu's proximity to the prison does not prove it was him that the witnesses were speaking about, but it is highly relevant. He had an almost near-continuous presence in Lapusnik. Witnesses spoke about seeing him every day or every two to three days in the neighbourhood near the Sopi compound, this is the compound where Celiku 3 was headquartered, it's the compound where the clinic was. And it's only 200 metres from the prison. The key point is this: The Trial Chamber failed to properly acknowledge the probative value of Isak Musliu's pseudonym Qerqiz, when considering the witnesses' accounts that they were beaten. And you asked -- Your Honours asked in the 30th of May memorandum as to whether parties agree that Isak Musliu used the pseudonym Qerqiz in the indictment period. I think I can confidently speak for the Defence on this matter, who I've spoken to before, and they have confirmed that they agree that this was his pseudonym at the relevant time. The Court heard no evidence to suggest that anyone else went by that name in that area at that time, and the Defence in their response appears to suggest that the Prosecution then had to prove the absence of another Qerqiz. Given that no witness or any document before the Court indicated the existence of another person in the area with this name, and indeed at no stage in the trial did the Defence even suggest that there was another one, we disagree. What the Prosecution, what we had to disprove, was the reasonable possibility that on the whole of the evidence the Qerqiz who witnesses mentioned was not him. Three witnesses testified as to being beaten or seeing others being beaten by a man wearing a mask who they came to know as Qerqiz, but by its own legally flawed approach, the Trial Chamber avoided reaching the inescapable conclusion that that person was Musliu. I'll refer very briefly to the evidence: L-12 was beaten by four people. He heard one of the beaters call another one who was masked Qerqiz. This is transcript 1808 to 9 and 1811. L-10 heard Shala address the masked person who beat him and mistreated another detainee also as Qerqiz. L-04 was regularly beaten by someone he came to know as Qerqiz because of being told by a fellow detainee that that masked person was from his hometown of Racak and his true name was Isak Musliu. The Trial Chamber failed to consider the cumulative effect of all this evidence, and in particular, to consider it in conjunction with three other witnesses: That is Witness Karpuzi and L-96, who saw Isak Musliu without his mask in the main house in the prison compound; and L-64, who saw him enter and leave, at one point taking off his mask as he did so. Now, the Trial Chamber made a clear error regarding Witness Karpuzi's evidence, and we've spoken about this in some length, we've written on this in some length in our appeal brief paragraphs 3.46 to 3.53 and it is not, in our submission, as the Defence would call it, it's not a harmless error. According to the Trial Chamber, Witness Karpuzi said that he was in the Gzim Gashi compound and he heard Musliu singing in the oda, this is the oda room in the prison compound across the road. This is not what Witness Karpuzi said. He testified that he was in the oda of the main house in the prison compound and he saw Musliu there, and indeed he sang along with him on more than one occasion. We do not suggest that Karpuzi specifically corroborates seeing Musliu beat L-04, L-10, L-12. We do not suggest he specifically corroborates Musliu's beating of L-96 or, indeed, seeing -- he does not specifically corroborate seeing, as L-64 did, Musliu going in and out of the prison. But he does provide very powerful general corroboration of Isak Musliu's presence in the prison. Now, the Trial Chamber articulated its concerns about the two witnesses, L-64 and 96, and they found they could not corroborate each other. We do not seek in this appeal to go behind the Trial Chamber's remarks about these witnesses in paragraphs 26 and 28, insofar as requiring that they be corroborated on material particulars. But notwithstanding those individual concerns, the important point is that now with Karpuzi's evidence we have the additional corroboration; in other words, Karpuzi corroborates both of them as to whether Musliu was in the camp at the time. And it's especially important to bear in mind that both times 96 -- both times Witness 96 saw Musliu, a man he knew from childhood, it was in the main house in the compound, albeit it was in the upstairs room of that compound and not in the oda in the downstairs part of that house. In this respect I should correct our appeal brief paragraphs 3.42 to 3.64 where we had indicated that the oda room was upstairs. We have verified it was downstairs. Finally, any reservations the Trial Chamber may have had about Witness L-96, about his honesty and reliability on this issue, based on any evidence suggesting Musliu was in Rahovec was unjustified. We are not misunderstanding what the Trial Chamber has done here. We understand the Trial Chamber is not finding that he had a continuous presence in Rahovec; we're pointing out, rather, that the Trial Chamber had reservations about Witness 96 for this reason, that it could not dismiss the finding that suggested that he may have been in Rahovec and that this affected their -- when they came to analyse Witness L-096's credibility, this was wrong. The dates when L-096 was in the prison are not incompatible with any evidence suggesting Musliu was in Rahovec, and even if Musliu was there, in Rahovec, it would not preclude him being in Lapusnik on the same day. I'll finish my submissions on this point here, Your Honours. Drawing all of these strands together, the inescapable conclusion is that Musliu was the masked person who beat detainees in the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, Karpuzi testified that Musliu sang in the oda, in the compound, during the war, but it is not clear to me from his testimony that it necessarily fell to the period, to the month, when prisoners were in the compound, as opposed to sometime before the prisoners got there. So could you point to specific evidence, please, that Musliu sang in the oda, in the Lapusnik/Llapushnik prison during the months that prisoners were found to be in the compound.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't point to the specific evidence. I looked myself to see whether that evidence was there. The actual month was not referred to in Witness Karpuzi's evidence. He didn't say specifically June/July. However, what I can say is that the entire questioning of Karpuzi was done on the basis that Karpuzi was giving his evidence about the events at the time. That's as specific as I can do -- assist you with, Your Honour. I -- yes. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Brady. I just thought that it would be fair that we are aware of the fact that Karpuzi's evidence did not contain those specific time references that would have been helpful to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: It would have been helpful if that question had been asked and he was asked specifically the month; however, our submission is the clear import of his testimony is that he was speaking about the relevant time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, I have a question which is more by way of a comment, and in this I borrow liberally from something that Judge Meron has said and with it, I believe, you concur. It is this, that an appeals court has a tendency to defer to the findings of fact made by the Trial Court. Would you say that this is especially so in the delicate field of identification? If that is so, would you accept that your case is presenting the Appeals Court with the extraordinary challenge of concluding that in that delicate field of identification in which the Trial Court saw and heard all the witnesses, that nevertheless the Trial Court erred?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: We would definitely agree with Your Honour that the Appeals Chamber would generally defer to findings of fact in what you call the delicate field of identification. This is a -- this is a classic Trial Chamber function of assessing credibility, reliability of witnesses, of giving it weight. However, here our submission is that the error is much more far-reaching. The error is in failing to draw properly together other evidence, other strands of evidence, in addition to, as you mention, the identification evidence, and to consider it as a whole. Now, we also acknowledge that this case presents what you call an extraordinary challenge to this Chamber because you would essentially have to make these findings yourselves and that is not an easy task and we acknowledge that. However, a review of the transcript and, I could also add, assisted by a complete record of the transcript being kept on the videotapes, we believe that this Chamber could be in an equal position to make that -- to make those findings yourselves. That is why at the beginning of my submissions I referred to two alternative possibilities: Either that this Chamber reviews the evidence itself, necessarily that would include all of the record; or, because of the pervasiveness of the errors that it was sent -- that it was remitted back for a new trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Ms. Brady. We break now and we resume in half an hour, in 30 minutes, to conclude the submissions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, we resume our hearing and I will give the floor again to the Prosecutor to conclude their submissions. I note you have -- sorry. Yes, Judge Schomburg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You are far better placed than me to answer this legal question. Does it have any impact only the assessment of evidence that Karpuzi was declared a hostile witness because of inconsistencies between his prior statements and his oral testimony in assessing the evidence? Why was the distinction made? First, that's not the only one in the entire judgement that a witness is called a hostile witness, but is the result of this that there is a limitation in how far you can rely on the testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: If Your Honour would give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Because we are not in our system acquainted to call a witness a hostile witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this might be something I need to check, but my understanding is that Karpuzi was not declared a hostile witness in the same way that Buja and Behluli, for example, were declared hostile to the Prosecution. It would be one factor, his -- if he had given a different statement beforehand and then he gives evidence in court, it could be one factor to be taken into account. However, we would submit that the sworn testimony on this point about seeing Mr. Musliu in the oda is not affected by that prior statement. And in fact, I would like to give a further answer to -- and tied in with the answer I gave previously to Judge Meron. If you look at his earlier statement which was admitted as P136, admitted into evidence, in this statement Mr. Karpuzi said that he visited Lapusnik, the prison, during the last month in July, that that was his -- his testimony was that he was in the house in the last month of July. So when Judge Meron asked, Is there other evidence to support the timing of his sighting of Musliu, it does exist in this statement. And I should also add a further amplification, that the evidence of Mr. Karpuzi is that on the 29th of May Celiku 3 moved to the Gzim Gashi compound so that his evidence, his evidence about the sightings is occurring after that move, so after, post-29 May. That can be seen from paragraph 693 of the trial judgement and his transcript pages 3093 to 95 and 3248 to 49. So those two matters, in our submission, compel the inference that the period of time he was talking about were the period under discussion. I hope that assists, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I only want to facilitate your research. It's to be found on the transcript of 8 February 2005, pages 3158 to 3165, and in the judgement, para 768.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll review those transcript references --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: -- and perhaps in the reply I can provide a further answer. Can I make an inquiry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Brady, to what extent were these prior statements admitted? Were they admitted only to establish that there was a contradiction in the oral testimony of the witness or were they admitted as evidence in itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, this is -- they were given an exhibit -- they were given an exhibit number to suggest that they were an admitted piece of evidence in this case, P136, but they were moved into evidence because of their extensive use in cross-examination. And this was something the Defence did not object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Brady, you may proceed with your submissions now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: May I clarify one thing before I finish on the Musliu -- Prosecution's appeal against Mr. Isak Musliu. We were aware from the Scheduling Order that the Prosecution had 30 minutes from 11.00 until 11.30 left for the submissions. And in view of a little bit of late start that we had and the number of questions which, of course, we have to factor into when making our submissions, but also out of a concern that we do address your questions properly on JCE, specifically Mr. Wirth will be doing that, I will ask for the Court's indulgence that instead of the 30 minutes, that we in fact be allowed an extra ten minutes in our submissions now. And I would -- in saying that, I do not think the Prosecution will need as much time as has been allotted in the reply, we've been allotted 45 minutes. I don't think that we will need that amount of time. So it would be taking off from our reply to make these submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Actually, you had only 25 minutes left, but it's granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Much appreciated. I'll turn now to the final ground of appeal that the Prosecution brings against Isak Musliu in terms of -- before dealing with the JCE of course, but in terms of his command of the prison and KLA soldiers operating there. This is the error in not finding that Musliu had a position of effective control over the prison and the KLA guards and soldiers operating in it in paragraph 715. This is amply set out in our appeal brief so I can be quite short in my oral submissions, but in effect, the Trial Chamber made two factual errors about his command position and neither of which a reasonable trier of fact could have made. And upholding either error would compel the finding that he had control over the prison or, at the very least, the Celiku 3 soldiers and guards who worked in it. The first error was in not finding that the Celiku 3 unit ran, that they operated the prison, or at least that members of the Celiku 3 performed duties in the prison. And this error arises not so much -- Your Honours do not need to go so much to the evidence but to the logic of the Trial Chamber's own factual findings. Firstly, the -- this prison was a KLA-run prison, and on the Trial Chamber's own findings involved at least some degree of organisation and coordination. Detainees were kept locked up, many were chained, there was guards, there was a system where they could be fed and taken to the toilet. The detainees often, when they were released, got similar instructions upon their release, what they should say about their detention there. And in fact, the very conviction of Bala and Bala's conviction underscore that this was, at least on some level, some kind of supervised KLA operation. Now, if we consider that fact together with the fact found by the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 702 and 703, that effectively the Celiku 3 unit was the only unit which was effectively stationed and operating south of the Peje-Prishtine road. Then no other reasonable inference is open but that the Celiku 3 was the one who had, let's call it, the job of running the prison. Simply put, there were no other candidates for doing so, and in our submission the Trial Chamber unreasonably found out in the possibility that an essentially phantom unit was operating the prison. A particularly critical oversight was the Trial Chamber just did not make findings on the active presence and the active participation -- let me say that again. Did not make a finding about what unit, what KLA unit, Mr. Bala was actually in, and they made findings throughout the judgement about his very active presence and participation in the prison. But because they didn't make this finding about his unit, essentially then it meant to the Trial Chamber did not have or did not consider the regular and consistent involvement of at least this one KLA Celiku 3 soldier in the prison and the logical implication that flows that the Celiku 3 was at least involved in the running of the camp. To put it very shortly, the nature of the prison; the fact that Celiku 3 was the only operational unit south of the road; the fact that the Celiku 3 members, such as Mr. Bala, worked there; in light of the finding that the Trial Chamber actually found Mr. Musliu to have at least a position of effective command over Celiku 3 units, that's in paragraph 712; and given the submissions I've already made about his presence there, the only reasonable conclusion is that he was in a position of effective control over the prison and the KLA guards and soldiers working there, at least those in the Celiku 3 unit. And apart from Bala there was other evidence of other guards actively present there such as the guard known as Tamuli and the guard known as Salihi and we've pointed out this evidence in our brief so I need not say more. Finally, there was the second error relating to Musliu's command, the Trial Chamber not finding that Musliu was not the overall commander of Celiku 3 unit, at least the part of Lapusnik lying below the road. I think that we have covered this at length in our appeal brief and we set out the evidence which, in our submission, compels this finding and I won't repeat it. In conclusion, there is no other reasonable conclusion but that Isak Musliu was the person witnesses referred to as the beater Qerqiz in the prison. He was in effective command and control of the prison and the KLA guards there, and we ask you to uphold both grounds 1 and 2 of the Prosecution's appeal against him. Unless Your Honours have questions, I'll now hand over to Mr. Wirth, who will address you on the Prosecution's third ground of appeal regarding joint criminal enterprise and he'll also address you briefly on the findings this Chamber would need to make in order to convict Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu under either Article 7(1) or 7(3). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Lapusnik prison case is a classical camp case. All requirements of joint criminal enterprise of the second category are present in this case. First, a plurality of persons. The camp was run by a plurality of persons and the Trial Chamber found that it was the KLA who ran the camp, and that is in paragraph 282. Second, an organised criminal system. This requirement is fulfilled by the finding that there was a culture of violence in the camp, paragraph 726. Third, a common criminal purpose, the requirement is fulfilled by the finding that the camp was an example of the coordinated and organised nature of the targeting of suspected collaborators, judgement paragraph 217. Fourth, contributions. The requirement of contributions is fulfilled inter alia by the finding that KLA soldiers beat the victims on a daily basis, paragraphs 291 and 294. And fifth, knowledge and intent to further the criminal system. It is self-evident that this requirement is fulfilled since the KLA members running the camp knew of the criminal system they created and they created it through their own conduct and they also knew of their contributions, which were intentional. Despite these facts, the Trial Chamber did not find that a JCE existed, and it had essentially two concerns. First, it considered that the members of the JCE were insufficiently identified. This concern is unfounded, since the JCE members were identified as they were pled, namely, as the three respondents and other KLA soldiers and guards at the camp. The Trial Chamber's view that the JCE members must be defined more narrowly is erroneous and wrong. The Trial Chamber's second concern was the perceived possibility that crimes in the camp might have been committed by rogue elements, rogue elements who did not share the common purpose. This concern is unfounded; it has no basis in the evidence. Now, I propose that in the following I will run you through all five elements of joint criminal enterprise and set out why the requirements are present. In so doing, I will discuss the Trial Chamber's concerns in detail in regard with the elements to which they belong. I will also address in my submissions the Appeals Chamber's third question since this question relates to the element of common purpose -- sorry, since this element relates to common purpose -- this question relates to common purpose, I will address it in this context. I begin with the plurality of persons. The plurality of persons in the present case was pled and proven as consisting of the three respondents and other KLA soldiers and guards at the camp. First, all three respondents were present at the camp. For Mr. Bala this was found by the Trial Chamber, and Ms. Brady has just set out -- has just explained that Mr. Limaj and Mr. Musliu were also present at the camp. Second, the remainder of the persons operating the camp were KLA soldiers and guards at the camp and this is clear from the Trial Chamber's repeated findings that the KLA ran the camp and that the KLA detained the victims. This is further illustrated by the fact that Mr. Bala and Murrizi, two KLA soldiers, were found to have been guards at the camp. Despite these findings, the Trial Chamber failed to conclude that a plurality of persons existed. And the reason for this failure was an incorrect legal approach. The Trial Chamber found that identifying the members of the JCE as KLA members was insufficient. Instead, it required a showing that the JCE members belonged to a more narrowly defined and more specific group. However, there is no such requirement among the elements of JCE. JCE members must not belong to some narrowly defined group; rather, all that needed to be proven in this case was that the JCE members belonged to the group which was pled in the indictment, namely, KLA soldiers and guards at the camp, and this has been proven and therefore the element of plurality of persons is fulfilled. I come to the next element. The camp also constituted an organised criminal system. The Trial Chamber found that there was cultural violence at the camp, that conditions under which most of the victims were detained amounted to cruel treatment, that the victims were beaten on a daily basis by KLA soldiers, that prisoners in the cow-shed were continuously beaten by KLA soldiers at the camp, and that the detainees lived in constant fear of physical abuse, if not death. An organised criminal system has been established. The next element which I will address is the element of common purpose. Since this element is the most important element in the present case, I need to address it in some detail. In so doing, I will first deal with the Appeals Chamber's third question, since this question regards common purpose. I will then run through the -- sorry, I will then turn to the Trial Chamber's concern that the common purpose could be in doubt because of the hypothetical existence of rogue elements in the camp. I begin with Your Honours' third question. The third question asked whether the common purpose in this case is limited to the victim groups as pled in the indictment, namely, to Serb civilians and perceived Albanian collaborators, and our answer to that question is: Yes. We are bound to our pleading and we are thus bound to the victim groups as pled. We also agree with the Appeals Chamber that our appeals brief is not entirely clear on that point; however, this does not detract from the fact that we did prove what we pled in this case, namely, that the common purpose was targeting Serb civilians and perceived Albanian collaborators. I will now in a first step show that the victims fell within the two groups which were pled, and I will then in a second step show that the JCE members shared the common purpose to target these exact groups. I begin with the showing that almost all Serbs in the camp were civilians. As is clear from the manner in which they were targeted -- sorry, in which they were captured, all Serb victims were targeted as civilians. Stamen Genov was arrested from a civilian bus together with three other Serbs; all wore civilian clothes. Indeed, according to the evidence most of the ten Serbs in the camp were civilians. There are only two exceptions, Miodrag Krstic, for whom no evidence exists, and Stamen Genov, who was a soldier, and his military ID was only discovered by the KLA after he had been arrested during the first incident of mistreatment. Now, the fact that those two cannot be shown to be civilians should not trouble the Appeals Chamber. The reason is that the Defence was specifically notified in paragraph 42 of the pre-trial brief, filed seven months before the proceedings, that the Prosecution no longer claimed that all Serbian victims were civilians but only that almost all were civilians. This paragraph explicitly identifies Stamen Genov as a soldier. In conclusion, all Serbs, including Stamen Genov and Miodrag Krstic, fell into the category which was pled and of which the Defence was notified. I turn to the Albanian victims and I will show that all of them were perceived collaborators. Most importantly, the Trial Chamber found the following: Those detained in the camp were principally if not solely, those who were or who were suspected of being Serbians or Kosovo Albanians who collaborated with the Serb authorities, and that's in paragraph 174. As mentioned, the Trial Chamber also found that the camp itself was an example of the coordinated and organised nature of the targeting of suspected collaborators, and that is in paragraph 217 of the judgement. There is ample circumstantial evidence which shows that only perceived collaborators were brought to the camp. For example, when Shukri Buja was approached by a father whose son had arrested, what did Shukri Buja do? He went to the camp and he explained that the son was not a collaborator, and that is how he achieved the release of the son. Shukri Buja also tells us that it was sufficient that a person was suspected of being a collaborator for being arrested and checked, and this evidence can be found in Exhibit P160 on pages 64 and 66 to 67. Another witness, Witness L-64, testified about the camp's inmates as follows: "They were arrested for either having worked with the Serb government or they were suspected of continuing to work with them since the 1980s and the 1990s." And that's at transcript page 4463. Now, this testimony is corroborated by a plethora of further evidence which is referred to in 2.287 and 2.289 of the appeals brief. In summary, the evidence clearly shows that the Albanian victims in the camp were perceived collaborators and that the Serb victims were civilians. Your Honours, we have prepared a list with evidence regarding the groups of victims in the camp, and I propose that in order to supplement our answer to your third question which I just gave to you, we will provide you with that list after the hearing. May I ask whether that is agreeable?
