utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now go on to explain that not only did the victims fall into the victim group, the evidence also proves that the JCE members shared the common purpose to target these victims. Now, the Serbian victims were simply held and mistreated on the basis of their ethnicity, and that is clear from the random manner in which they were picked from public buses and private cars. As regards the Albanian victims, there is ample direct evidence that the KLA soldiers committing the mistreatment had the purpose to target perceived collaborators. For example, masked soldiers asked L-10 about spies in his village. He also asked him whether Emin Emini, an inmate of the camp was a spy. KLA soldiers Ali Gashi and Ramadan Behluli beat L-06 and asked him why he was selling wood to the Serbs and also asked him to talk about spies. Another victim in the camp was beaten by unidentified KLA soldiers because he had translated for a Russian journalist. Now, the three respondents shared the common purpose which transpires from the conduct which I just described. This is the only conclusion that can be drawn from their important positions in the camp and from their active contributions to it. I will address the contributions in more detail later, but in a nutshell Mr. Limaj decided who should be detained; Mr. Musliu was the immediate commander of the camp; and Mr. Bala had the keys. I conclude, the Prosecution pled and proved that the common purpose which was shared by the JCE members was the targeting of Serb civilians and perceived Albanian collaborators. But despite this, despite the clear evidence, the Trial Chamber refused to find that a common purpose existed and this brings me to my submissions about the concerns which prevented the Trial Chamber from making this finding. The concern was that the Trial Chamber considered that it could not rule out that some crimes in the camp were committed by so-called opportunistic visitors or by KLA soldiers who were not motivated by the KLA's policy but by personal revenge. This conclusion is not founded upon the evidence. Now, we explained in our brief where the testimony of Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen does not support the Trial Chamber's finding, in addition highly relevant evidence clearly shows that it was impossible for rogue elements to be in the camp. After the 9th of May, 1998, Lapusnik and its vicinity was controlled by a KLA force of increasing strength. KLA soldiers were positioned in the village and accommodated in various private houses in the village. The prison camp was a narrowly confined compound and it was guarded by KLA soldiers. The prisoners themselves were locked up in prison rooms and only KLA guards had the keys to these prison rooms. In addition, many prisoners were tied or chained to the wall. In short, the detainees were tied and locked away in a narrowly confined camp run by the KLA in a village full of KLA soldiers, in a territory controlled by the KLA. To assume that anything could have happened to these detainees which the KLA didn't want to happen to them is unreasonable and not based on the evidence. I don't have time to go through that, but I would also refer Your Honours to the Tadic appeal judgement which, we submit in a very similar case, overturned the Trial Chamber in Tadic. And we referred to that in our appeal brief. Now, in conclusion, the evidence provides no basis and leaves no room for the Trial Chamber's rogue elements hypothesis. The Appeals Chamber should reject it as unreasonable. However, the Trial Chamber's position is not only factually untenable, it is also legally irrelevant, and the reason is that even when we consider for the sake of the argument that the rogue who entered the camp as an opportunistic visitor did commit one of the crimes, the members of the JCE could still be responsible for the rogue's crimes. This is the effect of the Kvocka appeals judgement. In this case the act of Zoran Zigic who was not a JCE member have been imputed to the accused Kvocka who was a JCE member, and this has been explicitly noted in footnote 885 of the Brdjanin appeal judgement. Thus, the Trial Chamber's rogue elements hypothesis, even if true, would not exonerate the JCE members. This concludes my discussion of the common purpose and I showed you two things. There was a common purpose to target Serb civilians and perceived Albanian collaborators, and the Trial Chamber's concerns, based upon its rogue elements hypothesis are without basis. Consequently, the element of common purpose is present in this case. I will now address the last two elements of JCE: Contribution and mens rea together. The JCE members including the three respondents contributed to the criminal system with knowledge of the system and with intent to further it. I begin with the respondents. Mr. Limaj contributed to the camp in a very substantial manner. He decided who should be detained and who should be released. For example, Witness L-06 testified that Fatmir Limaj told him this: "If you have done something, you will be killed. If you are innocent, you will go home," and you will find that on transcript page 1014, and it's referred in the judgement in paragraph 538. Further evidence shows that, indeed, it was Mr. Limaj who finally released L-06. Mr. Limaj was also involved in the release of L-07, Vojko Bakrac, Ivan Bakrac, L-04, L-10, and L-96. In addition, Mr. Limaj, as the overall commander of the area, also provided leadership for the camp's operation. Now, as regards the second respondent, Mr. Musliu, he contributed to the camp as the immediate commander and also by mistreating prisoners, and I refer you to the judgement in paragraphs 311, 3 -- 673 and 677. Finally, Mr. Bala's contributions are clear from the facts underlying his connection. In addition to these contributions, all three respondents had also the required mens rea. Indeed, their mens rea must be inferred from these contributions as well as from their important positions in the camp. These factors taken together allow no other reasonable conclusion but that they knew about the criminal system which they furthered and they did so intentionally. As regards other KLA soldiers and guards at the camp, many of their contributions have already been discussed and their mens rea must be inferred. This concludes my submission on JCE. I have shown that all requirements of JCE were present and it has been shown that the Trial Chamber's concerns were no valid basis for a refusal to make that finding. The Appeals Chamber should reverse the Trial Chamber's finding that there was no JCE. On this basis, I will now shortly address the appropriate remedy. The Appeals Chamber should take one of the measures set out by my colleague Ms. Brady at the beginning of her submissions. In case the Appeals Chamber chooses to decide the case itself, it should convict the respondents according to their crimes. In this case, as set out in our appeals brief, Mr. Limaj and Mr. Musliu should be convicted as members of the JCE 2 for torture and cruel treatment and under JCE 3 for murder. Alternatively, convictions under 7(3) should be entered for Mr. Limaj and Musliu. Mr. Bala's conviction should be revised and he should be convicted under JCE 2 for all crimes of torture and cruel treatment, and under JCE 3 for those murders which he did not commit himself. Mr. Bala's sentence should be revised accordingly. That brings me to the end of my submissions and I'm available for your questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I think I may be able to do it in three minutes. As Mr. Wirth has said, I will be addressing the sentence of Mr. Bala, Prosecution appeal. From mid-June to the end of July, 23 men were held in subhuman conditions in Lapusnik camp for up to six weeks. Some of these men were beaten, tortured, and killed. When the KLA was forced to evacuate, more than 20 of these mens were marched into the mountains, where nine of them were shot to death. Bala was one of the men who massacred these nine detainees; Bala marched them up into the mountains; he was responsible, with others, for the maintenance of the deplorable conditions in the camp; he held one detainee at gunpoint; he beat another until he lost consciousness; he forced detainees to bury corpses including one of a fellow detainee; he assisted others in acts of beating and torture. For this direct and active role in these very serious crimes the Trial Chamber imposed a sentence of 13 years which was manifestly inadequate and in our submission constitutes an error in discretion. Other cases before this Tribunal, for the same conduct, have imposed graver penalties and apart from our discussion in the brief in paragraphs 444 and following, I would like to refer you to the case of Mitar Vasiljevic where this Chamber imposed a sentence of 15 years for aiding and abetting the execution of five men, and cruel treatment of a further two. Like Bala, Vasiljevic was not a commander. His crimes were grave. He stood by a firing-squad, pointing his gun, preventing escape. However, unlike Bala he did not maintain a camp, he did not engage in cruel treatment, and he did not personally commit the executions. The Vasiljevic Trial Chamber considered a number of aggravating factors in paragraph 276 of the judgement, such as verbal abuse, long-term suffering, and cold-blooded murders. However, in this case the Trial Chamber in paragraph 731 of the judgement considered that similar factors should not be considered an aggravation because they were considered in the gravity of the offence. These were: Vulnerability of the victims, the violent nature of the acts, and the circumstances generally. However, when you look at the Trial Chamber's discussion of the gravity, these factors are not properly articulated. There's no mention that the victims were weak and captive, no detail about the inherent cruelty, and no detail about the deplorable conditions. Bala's active role in the executions should have been the primary consideration; however, the Trial Chamber did not consider it in any detail. The factors lessening his gravity, such as lack of command, acting under orders, and sadistic motive were given too much weight instead. Sadistic motive -- the absence of a sadistic motive is irrelevant. His lack of command in light of the protected values such as the life and integrity of the mental and physical wealth of the victims were at large violated, and the Trial Chamber considered this in Vasiljevic in paragraphs 302 following and said that under these circumstances, a low status could not have a mitigating effect. Finally, acting under orders should not have been given too much weight. This Chamber said in Bralo, in paragraph 24 of the appeals judgement, that it is the duty of any person involved in a armed conflict to comply fully with norms of international law and if they are pressured to participate, there remains a legal and moral obligation to act in accordance. Bala had this obligation and failed it. Even if he did act under orders, this factor should have been had no or little effect in light of his criminal conduct. He was a willing participator; he was not a bystander. In conclusion, his sentence does not reflect that the Trial Chamber properly considered the relevant factors and it does not do justice to the victims and the survivors, and it should be increased. Thank you, Your Honour, this concludes my submissions. Are there any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. May I just ask for clarification, seeing the time is now nearly five to 12.00. Do you wish me to go till roughly ten till 1.00 or stop at half past 12.00 and resume --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm much obliged. Makes more sense. May I, therefore, begin by indicating that what you have heard today from the Prosecution is essentially an attempt to do what they deny they are doing, which is to relitigate the trial in front of you. We realise this is a point we've made in the brief, but it is extremely important given the concessions that have been made by the Prosecution to see what the real ambit of this appeal is, as it certainly affects, in fact, all three accused. And the ambit I want to say and the parameters that have, in a sense, been conceded is set out in one sentence in the response by the Prosecution, received obviously after their main brief. I'll give you the paragraph number, it's just one sentence. I don't ask that it's looked up because the sentence speaks for itself. It's paragraph 117 in their response, and in that paragraph they say this: "The Prosecution accepts that the Trial Chamber did correctly state the standard of proof" - and there's additional words that are extremely important - "and the manner of its application." We say, therefore, one has to look extremely carefully to see whether truly there has been an error of law, never mind an error of fact in this case. Because, essentially what the Prosecution are saying is that the Trial Chamber didn't misstate the law, so there's no error of law in that sense, they understood the law, they stated it correctly, and how to apply it. But somehow, they claim, between the statement of the principles and their application - in other words, how they're applied - and their actual application in the same judgement which is almost in the same breath, the Trial Chamber has made a very gross error in not actually doing what they say they're doing. And we say this is impugning the Trial Chamber's integrity, essentially, because the Trial Chamber says it is doing precisely what is being criticised at the moment. So, for example, just to take the main elements that are being concentrated on. The Trial Chamber at no stage said that it was requiring a higher standard in this case and that therefore any doubt would do. And you will have noticed that nowhere has the Prosecution been able to illustrate to you that the Trial Chamber has incorporated, as it were, any doubt as opposed to any reasonable doubt. Now, this has been defined in many jurisdictions and I don't take time, but the obvious definitions are a fanciful doubt, an speculative doubt, an imagined doubt, a frivolous doubt. There's no suggestion in any of their argument that the Trial Chamber, as it were, has stooped to that kind of doubt. So essentially they repeat regularly throughout the judgement that it is beyond reasonable doubt, and in fact that the doubts that they have, we say, are within that range. Now, may I just pause for a moment because I'm going to ask for you to look at some passages in the trial judgement. I appreciate you've read it. I did ask if it was available to each of you today, I hope that it is in one form or another, but the -- the position here on review is extremely important because one's not dealing here with - and obviously as far as Limaj is concerned - with an appeal by a defendant against a conviction, where there has been, as it were, a firm conclusion drawn by the Trial Chamber. Where it is an appeal by the Prosecution, the standard of unreasonableness is the same, one appreciates that, but it -- when you apply that to a different process, one is the process of reaching a firm conclusion of conviction. The other one, which is this one, is a different process, it's a process wherein, as we shall see, the Trial Chamber is saying, We were unable to be satisfied. What the Prosecution then have to do is to say to you today, Well, when they say they were unable to be satisfied, that was outwith the normal range of reasonable decisions to be taken by a Tribunal because there was only one conclusion. Well, of course, there's a certain, if I may put it, irony amongst all of this if one just steps back for a moment because every time a Trial Chamber comes to a conclusion that they're unable to be sure and the Prosecution is saying, as they must be at the trial level, there is only one conclusion, are they automatically going to say, Ah, right, well they must have applied the wrong standard of proof here. They haven't applied -- they haven't done what they say they're doing because, they say, these defendants are guilty. And then they appeal and then they ask this Chamber effectively to conduct a re-trial in a situation which is totally impractical for a trial of this length to be reviewed, total transcript, total video, you would have to spend as much time as the trial did, almost, in doing it. It's totally impractical. So we say what has to be looked at very carefully here, particularly bearing in mind the element of deference, particularly bearing in mind the areas that were concerned in this case were - one phrase has been used - delicate, but there's identification and credibility of witnesses. Now, these are areas that are particularly pertinent for a Trial Chamber to assess, and that is why this Chamber, the Appeals Chamber, has given due deference in that field. So when one's looking through one has to be saying, well, has the Trial Chamber got it completely wrong? Are they wholly erroneous? Are they making a decision with regard to an acquittal that doesn't come within the range of decisions available when you acquit? And of course you're available -- you're aware of the range, it stems from or starts with at one end of the spectrum of the probably guilty, but that's not enough. Possibly guilty, but that's not enough. Might be guilty, but that's not enough. Right through to, well, we feel he was innocent, and that's not enough plainly. They're all the range of decisions, very different as I suggest it is to the approach that will be taken when looking at an appeal that has arisen out of a conviction, so there's a much bigger range and that is why we've asked you to have before I pass to the judgement, a quotation from a case with which you'll be familiar. And don't know whether it's -- I hope it's been handed up on a single sheet of paper. This case is, in fact, cited by the Prosecution itselves in a footnote in their brief, it's Rutaganda. May I just ask if that single sheet is available because it's paragraph 24. May I just read that, because it fits into this first point that I'm making. "The Appeals Chamber in Bagilishema held that the same standard of unreasonableness and the same deference to factual findings of the Trial Chamber apply when the Prosecution appeals against an acquittal. The Appeals Chamber will only hold that an error of fact was committed when it determines that no reasonable trier of fact could have made the impugned finding. Considering that it is the Prosecution that bears the burden at trial of proving the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, the significance of an error of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice is somewhat different when the error is alleged by the Prosecution." And it's this sentence that's important. "The Prosecution faces a more difficult task. It must show that, when account is taken of the errors of fact committed by the Trial Chamber, all reasonable doubt of the accused's guilt has been eliminated." And I would submit that this is another way of putting the same point that I've just been putting to you about the review of unreasonableness as applied to an acquittal where there is a range of decisions that can be taken, and you have to be, as it were, satisfied that this decision by the Trial Chamber is outwith that range of decisions available and open to the Trial Chamber. So just going back to the point I started with here. The Trial Chamber is not suggesting, therefore, a higher standard, that is, any doubt at any stage, and in fact their reasoning does not disclose that they used any doubt. Secondly, the Trial Chamber did not suggest at any stage that the evidence should be analysed or evaluated in isolation, which is another or the second point that the Prosecution are making. They repeatedly say throughout - and I shall illustrate in a moment - that they do give reasons as to why the combination is not satisfactory. Now, may I just pause on this second point. In Limaj's case, if I may distill it or boil it down to one or two things, liability in his case really can only be achieved by two routes. First route is by identifying him as playing a role at the camp. And plainly the Prosecution realise they do have to do that in order, certainly, if they're going to, as it were, establish JCE. So the identification of him there is extremely important. That's one route. Now, the other route is plainly the command responsibility: Was he in command of an area which included this camp? And that is the second main route. So those are the two main routes. Now, in relation to those, it's perfectly clear, we say, that the Trial Chamber had both in mind. Because they don't set out all the reasons every time they come to a conclusion doesn't mean to say they haven't considered them, but in fact they have considered them and they refer back to earlier paragraphs. So in fact, throughout this judgement they are saying they are looking at the whole of the evidence and in fact they are doing that. That's the second point. Now, the third point is they did not suggest that the process that they were involved in or they exercised applied - in other words, beyond reasonable doubt - applied only to predicated facts and not to the elements of the offence. This is the third point. This process is extremely important. What the Prosecution seem to be saying - I hope I haven't misunderstood today what they are saying - is that it's all right for the Trial Chamber to individually assess witnesses, but actually they shouldn't apply the standard of proof to those individual, in other words beyond reasonable doubt, to those individual witnesses. But we say the two are inextricably interwoven, and again your own experience in having to make judgements of this kind, particularly when it comes to identification, that what you are doing is saying to yourself, Can I be sure of this witness, looking at this witness's internal inconsistencies, comparison with other witnesses, and comparison with the evidence as a whole? So it's an exercise in which you would be perfectly entitled to say, Well, I might be sure of this witness if there were some other material; or, This witness is so shot through that I'm not even going to look at other material. So for example it's interesting that the Prosecution haven't really tried orally to resurrect what we would call a witness that is well worth forgetting and is really off the radar and that's L-96. He, in fact, was a dismal failure at trial and was plainly, as the -- as the Trial Chamber found in their general observations, incredible. They would have to look for other material in his case. He relates, and he's essentially the only witness as far as Limaj's concerned, that relates to the Berisa Mountains. And the reasons for his lying are set out in the judgement, so I don't need to go through it. And of course, in his case, looking for corroboration is extremely difficult, and that is why obviously the Trial Chamber wasn't looking at witnesses in isolation, they were looking at them as a whole and they were attempting to form a basis of reliability in the process of reaching a final conclusion, if they could, of being sure. So we would submit in general terms that this judgement is an impeccable and classic example of how to approach a difficult case such as this and I know each case is difficult on its own merits, a difficult case such as this with great care, setting out at each stage all the factors that need to be taken into account. And it beggars belief to then go on and say that the Trial Chamber itself didn't actually employ the methods that it set out. So, may I in that context -- I hope to do it in the time available because I appreciate you are aware of the judgement, but there are some important aspects of it that bear on all these principles that I've just laid out in our brief. If you have the judgement in front of you, may I ask you -- and what I'll do to save turning back to sections is to just chronologically go through some of the paragraphs that bear upon the issues about which you've asked questions today and about which the Prosecution's addressed you. One starts with paragraph 10 on page 4. This is the paragraph acknowledged by the Prosecution which succinctly sets out exactly what has to be done here and it comes halfway down. "The standard to be met for a conviction to be entered is that of proof beyond reasonable doubt," so there's not only doubt, reasonable doubt, set out. "Accordingly, the Chamber has determined in respect of each of the counts charged against each of the Accused, whether it is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt, on the basis of the whole of the evidence, that every element of that crime and the forms of liability charged in the Indictment have been established." I don't read the rest. That is a key sentence. It is set out -- couldn't be set out more clearly. And as you cast your eye down the page, this heading, "Considerations Regarding the Evaluation of Evidence," goes on for many pages and indicates as a contextual matter, that right at the beginning of the judgement they are aware, the Tribunal, Trial Tribunal, they are aware, they are alert of what it is they are supposed to be doing and how they're supposed to be doing it. And that, as I say, surfaces as we go through the headings for Limaj, there are only the two major ones: That is, actual individual participation at the camp and/or the command structure, basically. It surfaces again. And you'll see in paragraph 12: The Chamber has been required to weigh and evaluate the evidence presented by all the parties." And then over the page: "The matters call for careful scrutiny." Now what happens on the next page 5, in paragraph 13 onwards, as you will have read, is that they very carefully set out the variety of factors that bear upon this case. They start with statements by witnesses that are materially different, prior statements. As you've recently asked a question about the status of prior statements, may I just at this stage, to save repeating it as we go through, particularly hostile witnesses, part of our submissions in relation to the admission of prior statements was based on the fact that in some jurisdictions, as you will be aware, that a prior statement by a hostile witness as opposed to just a prior statement indicating a difference, but by a hostile witness, particularly in the United Kingdom, leads to this situation: Namely, that the previous -- this was the position, although it's changed recently, one of the approaches to this is to be very careful about using the prior statement as evidence of the truth. The approach used to be that the only employment of the previous statement is to assess the current evidence. Now, I'm not suggesting as a matter of law that applies here; merely that what the Trial Chamber did effectively was to approach it with care. And we say that's entirely appropriate and it's for the Trial Chamber to assess at the end of the day whether, if somebody has changed their account and the Trial Chamber suspects that they are lying on oath in the Chamber, that the Trial Chamber is then quite entitled to say, Well, as a result of that, it casts serious doubt on the credibility of any of the previous accounts because we've got someone here who's capable of telling lies. So that's actually what the Trial Chamber did when it came to looking at hostile witnesses but at this very early stage, it's setting out the difficulties of approaching prior statements and, for example, may I just highlight, since you've asked here and the Prosecution have asked you to view again video, for example, interviews of hostile witnesses, some suggested the differences were due to the method of questioning when the prior to statements made, in particular in several instances suggesting a lack of specificity as to the time-period being referred to in a particular question. The Chamber was able to accept this possibility in some but not all cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So all that the Trial Chamber is doing here, we say, quite properly is saying considerable care has to be taken with regard to prior statements and setting out the factors. And over the page, on page 6, paragraph 14, we get to the hostile witnesses issue. I'll pause just for a moment. It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I've just had a brief conversation with Mr. Bala. He begs the Chamber's indulgence and would like to know if it would be all right if he could leave the proceedings at this point not because he is objecting to anything and I know that he would like to stay and continue to listen, but he's reached a point where I think it's a bit much for him. I've had conversations with him and he's indicated that we can proceed in his absence. He has no objection to that. I had an -- I've had arguments with him about him coming in any event, but that's a different issue and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I have no problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With the Chamber's permission, if he could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I have no problem in excusing him if he doesn't feel well, and I understand that you are not objecting to the continuation of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Mansfield, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm on page 6, and really I can go fairly quickly through these paragraphs. We're still dealing with evaluation. Consideration is given to victim witnesses and the question of loyalty and honour. On the next page 7, 17 is a very important paragraph because it's setting out there familiar factors to all of you about the risks of misidentification and this case particularly revolves around misidentification. They're all set out at the bottom of the page -- in fact, they're all together. There are eight different factors indicated there, again familiar to you. And then on the next page, 19, the care that has to be taken over photo spreads, and, for example, again the factors that have to be borne in mind in relation to photo spreads, they're all set out at the bottom of the page. Then on the next page, 20, very important paragraph, having set out all these factors, I haven't gone through them all but there it is: "With particular regard to the evidence of the visual identification of each of the Accused by various witnesses, it is to be emphasised that," and here it is again, "like all elements of an offence, the identification of each Accused as a perpetrator as alleged must be proved by the Prosecution beyond reasonable doubt." The two, we say, run hand in hand. "This is to be determined, however, in the light of all evidence, bearing on the issue of identification, evidence both for and against." And then going further down, visual identification is but one piece of what may be relevant evidence in a particular case. "The ultimate weight to be attached to each relevant piece of evidence, including each visual identification where more than one witness has identified an Accused, is not to be determined in isolation. Even though each visual identification and each other relevant piece of evidence, viewed in isolation, may not be sufficient to satisfy the obligation of proof on the Prosecution, it is the cumulative effect of the evidence," in other words, "the totality of the evidence bearing on the identification of Accused -- an Accused, which must be weighed to determine whether the Prosecution has proved beyond reasonable doubt that each Accused is a perpetrator as alleged." It really couldn't be emphasised and highlighted more, and then there's more reference to cautious scrutiny and on the succeeding pages, a number of witnesses are picked out for their essential incredibility, L-96 featuring top of the list. He's in paragraph 26. I don't go through all of those. So may I pause for a moment. That's the introduction to this trial judgement. Very clear enunciation of principles and how to apply them. What has not been put before you today, I have not been critical, it cannot be done in the time, but I do want to, but this next section really bears upon the issue of command because it's repeatedly said, Oh, Fatmir Limaj was in charge of the area and so on. The big issue at the trial was he in charge of an area that included Lapusnik and there was evidence both ways on that particular issue. But in order to understand it, it is necessary, and of course, the Trial Chamber did it this way to put it all in a context and that comes at page 16, which is the emergence of the KLA. And I would submit, these paragraphs are not criticised, they're a true reflection of what was going on, and if I can summarize it, the position was that this was in very early days in the spring of 1998. Matters were evolving organically, slowly, much like a guerilla movement, if that's the comparison that was made, with cells operating in different places, operating secretly with a lack of communication between them all. And dealing with, to begin with, a reactive situation to Serb invasion, effectively. And the development, therefore, of the KLA is important to an understanding of where areas of responsibility could be attributed. And if you look - I just pick out some paragraphs because there's not time to read them all - paragraph 56 on page 22, "The forming of the KLA structure appears to have been a slow process which was affected by factors independent of the local leaders." And then in the paragraphs that come thereafter there are references to guerilla body on the next page, small groups operating in various zones, the creation of brigades, and so on. And paragraph 60 on page 24, again illustrates the difficulty that was facing the Trial Chamber and it's too glib and too easy for the Prosecution to say now that it's clear; it isn't clear and wasn't clear then in the very early days. And they pick out the testimony of two individuals and of course their credibility on various things has been questioned, both of them, well, one doesn't doubt that but one sees the point they are making. A part of the division line between the subzones of Drenica in the north and Pastrik or Pashtrik went along the road, the Pristina highway, and Behluli drew on a map the boundaries of his zone, which as he explained reflected the situation after August 1998 and then the boundary drawn by Ramadan Behluli and so on. So they're looking very carefully at all of this. And then at paragraph 61, having looked very carefully at the various evidence that has been given, this is one of their conclusions. "There is an abundance of evidence to the effect that a boundary between areas of responsibilities of various units went along" - that - "highway. This is not, however, indicative of there being a zone border going along the highway, as the units on both sides of the road might have been in the same zone. It is not unlikely that at some point in time the border between Pastrik," further in the south and Drenica in the north, "did go along the highway. Nonetheless, the evidence is too scarce and contradictory for a definite finding to be made." And I don't read the rest of it. It's just to indicate that this was a highly contentious area and paragraph 65 which comes at the end of this section: "While the formation of Brigades and Battalions at various times in the second half of 1998 represents a further and significant stage in the progressive development of a more formalised and a more typical military type structure, it should not be imagined that they were descriptive of a body of soldiers of the numerical strength typically to be found in Brigades and Battalions," and so on. "Many KLA Brigades and Battalions even in the summer of 1998, when first formed, were little more than a shell to which soldiers were recruited or transferred at various times; typically they comprised the existing KLA points," which were just, as you know, positions that were taken up, some of them in Lapusnik itself. And another contextual matter, I move on further in the judgement, in terms of the command, it's relevant to command before one starts making assessments of who's got it right comes at paragraph 94 onwards. It's more material and this is 14 pages on the organisation of the KLA and the General Staff, its position and so on. And these -- and rather than read through them or even ask you to flick through them merely to -- before any assessment is made of the individual witnesses in relation to Fatmir Limaj, perhaps the summary of this section is at 132, paragraph 132. "In the Chamber's finding, this evidence," that's the evidence about the organisation of the KLA, "this evidence does not establish the nonexistence of a KLA organisational structure. Rather, it reflects the conditions under which the KLA operated at the time. The KLA was effectively an underground organisation, operating in conditions of secrecy out of concern to preserve its leadership, and under constant threat of military action by Serbian forces. The members of the General Staff did not meet regularly because of the security situation and identified themselves not by their names but by numbers for the same reason." That's important in relation to Limaj and various public appearances. "In these circumstances, it is of no surprise that the organisational structure and the hierarchy of the KLA were confusing, or not known, to outside observers, and that, to some, this suggested a state of confusion." And then over the page they deal with other factors bearing on the issue they were considering, armed conflict and intensity of conflict, on the succeeding pages. So those contextual matters set out over those headings are extremely important, I won't go back to them, but they set the scene for the later assessment in relation to command. In other words, this was an infant embryonic situation, fluid, and far from settled and it was not possible draw clear lines to indicate who was in charge of what, and in fact as you will have seen in the trial judgement there are plain references to another commander in the area of Lapusnik and it wasn't Fatmir Limaj. Now, coming to the individual points in the headings in the judgement and how they dealt with the first route to liability, namely, the individual liability, you will find that at page 188. In other words, I'm not taking you through the findings in relation to cruel treatment and murder and so on. In general terms, take you straight to the question of individual liability. That starts at 188 and a particular sequence, an important sequence, is at 195. Key question at 19 -- page 195, paragraph 530. The question that the Tribunal has said itself is the key and most important question: Was Fatmir Limaj identified at the prison camp? And the witnesses are then set out. The Prosecution are really only bothering with six now, so that's L-96, as I've said is no longer -- doesn't appear to be worthy of consideration. But there are -- the account that the Tribunal gives of their evidence, we suggest, that is of the other six, is accurate. And in particular, I'm not going to read out their account of what they said, but what is important is how did the Chamber assess their reliability. And taking the first two, that's the father and son, the Bakrac two, paragraph 534 is the -- one of the key paragraphs, there's a section here. And it's very extensive. From 534 onwards, extensive consideration is given to the approach to these witnesses, given that they were regarded, as it says in 534, as honest. There are circumstances -- and may I just pause. The Chamber must have had in mind all the observations that they made right at the beginning about the vulnerabilities and fallibilities of identification when they were doing this particular paragraph. "There are circumstances, however, which can render the evidence of a particular witness unreliable even though that evidence was given in a perfectly honest fashion. In this case, in particular, the events which both Ivan and Vojko Bakrac went through at the camp were extremely traumatic. They occurred some years ago. In the intervening years, Ivan Bakrac, and possibly Vojko Bakrac, have been influenced by television and internet coverage, in which it appears that Fatmir Limaj was depicted." May I pause there. The whole point about the publicity that was given to Fatmir Limaj and the question of transposing images and so on can occur in a variety of ways. First of all, plainly, you may think when you see the image after you've been released that that is what you saw at the time, either on television at the time or in the camp at the time. Quite honestly, because of course he had a role, in the sense that he was at Klecka and there was a press conference at Klecka and you've heard about that particular instant in June, the problem is that when somebody, particularly once the war is over, is given as much attention as he is, then you may retrospectively think that person back into a situation where you were at the time. And you may even think that you recognised him at the time because you may even think that's the person that you'd seen in earlier coverage. So there's a real risk where there is a traumatic event that has taken place before, and you obviously are concerned about the responsibility of those who may have incarcerated you. Therefore, what the Chamber goes on to say: "These considerations may well bear, in the Chamber's view, upon the ability of either or both of them to reliably identify one or more of the Accused. It is therefore necessary to look with particular scrutiny at their evidence." And then, in fact, we say, in the succeeding paragraphs 535, they do look with particular scrutiny. And one of the interesting points that they're making which -- in 535, if you just look at that. It isn't just a question of, well, did they recognise this particular person in a particular way? In fact, one of the conclusions -- and we say this is utterly within the range of reasonable decisions to be made by the Tribunal. This is not any old reason. This is not the Tribunal, as it were, applying a different standard of proof, and we say that what they've done here is to say because the incidents that the two are talking about are different, "It appears to the Chamber," this is on the next page, "that these two are either referring to different 'commanders,' or have different recollections of the time and context in which their encounters with the 'commander' occurred." So you see at once the difficulties here. And of course neither of these two actually picked out Fatmir Limaj with regard to the photo spreads and so on, and that's mentioned both in 536 and 537. And the -- in the middle of 537: "... when shown a clear photograph of Fatmir Limaj when clean-shaven, which is how Ivan Bakrac recalled the 'commander' appeared to him in Lapusnik, Ivan Bakrac did not recognise the 'commander.'" In other words, this is -- this is all very well for saying all these witnesses picked him out; in fact, they didn't. That was the point. It was a very confused situation which one understands, one doesn't want to be hypercritical of that situation. Rather than given the time go through each of the witnesses, but in fact each of the witnesses are considered in a similar way. So, for example, if you turn to page 540 -- sorry, paragraph 540 on page 202, L-06 and L-10 are set out there and the reservations, again, of the Tribunal: "It is the reliability of the process by which L-06 and L-10 have come to subsequently recognise Fatmir Limaj on television as the man in Lapusnik which remains of concern to the Chamber. The encounters ... each lasted only a few minutes." The descriptions by the two witnesses don't match; one with a beard and not having a beard, and you will recall a lot of material about that. So that L-04 is dealt with on the next page, 203, there are reservations about him. They are all expressed in paragraph 542, 543, failure to mention meetings and so on. Extensive reservations, the reservations on L-04, paragraph 542, 543, 544, all those are reservations. I mention them because when we get to the conclusions, of course what happens is that the Trial Chamber is referring back to all these reasons that they've given in each case, including the next one, which is L-07 and Shukri Buja's account, which is different. The reservations on L-07 come at 549. Now, once again, we say, it's very interesting how careful the Trial Chamber is. You see it at 550. "Having given careful consideration to all of these factors," this is in relation to L-07, "whilst L-07 was honest in his evidence despite the difficulties identified, and while his identification might be correct, the Chamber is unable to be satisfied that his identification of Fatmir Limaj as the person he knew in Lapusnik ... as ... Celiku is reliable." So once again, they can't do everything at once. They're taking each one very carefully and saying, as they're entitled to do, we don't find that we're satisfied with the reliability. I don't trouble with L-96 for the reasons I've already given. There are a lot of reservations about him in all the paragraphs that come after that. And they do make reference, obviously, to Fatmir's own evidence in relation to this which can't be overlooked. He did give evidence extensively about these matters. So the conclusions, the evaluation, come at paragraph 560. I'm sorry to have taken a little time to get there, but it's the first few words you may note there in 560. "For reasons given above" -- and they've given them and I've rattled through them, I'm afraid, rather fast but that's -- they've set them all out: "For reasons given above, the Chamber is not able to accept any of the individual identifications made by these various witnesses of Fatmir Limaj to be a reliable identification on the basis of which the Chamber could find, beyond reasonable doubt, that Fatmir Limaj was the person they saw, or knew as Celiku, in the Lapusnik prison camp, or in the Berisa Mountains..." Well, that's really only L-96. But they don't stop at that as you see in the next paragraph, and in fact extensively -- and I'll go as quickly as possible. "The Chamber has also considered the combined effect of these several identifications to determine whether they, or some of them, in combination displaced the risks of mistake in the individual identifications, so as to establish beyond reasonable doubt that Fatmir Limaj was that person. While accepting that a multiplicity of identifications by a variety of persons, at different times and in different circumstances, may, in a particular case, be enough to negate the risk of honest mistake present in respect of each separate identification when it is considered separately, that is neither a common nor a simple exercise. In the present case, the difficulties stipulated with respect to a number of the identifications, and the nature of the risk of mistake for each respective identification, are of such significance" - and that's for the Trial Chamber, we say, eminently to decide and assess, and deference enters the arena at that point - "in the Chamber's considered view, that, notwithstanding the strong possibility" - so that's within the range, again in relation to an acquittal - "the strong possibility apparent on the evidence, it is on final analysis not able to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt," and so forth. Indeed, they make an opposite point which is of interest here. "Indeed, rather than strengthening an identification of the man purported to be Celiku, the combined effect of the evidence serves to highlight the extent of the uncertainties and inconsistencies prevalent in the body of evidence relevant to this issue." And then perhaps I don't need to read out the reasons they give for the combination of difficulty, and what they've put in the middle here is - and I just read this part of it out, in 562: "It is significant that the two witnesses who potentially had the most extensive contact with the 'commander'" - that's the two Bakracs - "gave inconsistent physical descriptions of the person they saw in the prison camp and could not positively identify the commander from respective photo spreads." And then, "When all the separate physical descriptions provided by the witnesses are considered cumulatively, instead of the emergence of any striking similarities" - now, you will note the Prosecution today have tried to say there were striking similarities in their favour and we say, no, there weren't, and in fact, when you look and examine at the witnesses individuals you begin to get a very chequered pattern of descriptions and identifications. In fact they give the range there: "Specifically, descriptions of the 'commander's' face range from cleanshaven to the presence of a small beard, a medium-sized beard, a beard of two or three weeks' growth. Therefore, rather than reducing the risk of mistake evident in the individual identifications, their comparison leads to further uncertainty." But that isn't the end of it either. What are the Prosecution saying? All of this is lip-service to this exercise? We say that that is an insult to the Trial Chamber. They, absolutely, Trial Chamber, we say, were rigorous in saying this is a critical issue, paragraph 563, and they're worried about the constant exposure of Fatmir Limaj publicly in the images and the unconscious influence that that may expose witnesses to after the event and at the time. "Because of that risk" - this is 563 - "much care was necessary with the process of subsequent identification," and so on. "Further, particular care is called for on the part of the Chamber in assessing whether, having regard to that and the other known risks of mistake with the various identifications discussed earlier, and in the light of all other relevant evidence" - so again, they're looking at everything - "the Chamber is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt ... " And then they come to their conclusion which I don't need to read out. So on the individual matters we say that is the most exhaustive and comprehensive and detailed approach to their task that could be imagined by a Trial Chamber and there is really, we say, no lacuna in that reasoning so I turn, in the last ten minutes, to the other root to liability, which is command, and once again the Trial Chamber has set the key question. It is on page 214.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Schomburg has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before turning to another issue I just want to put a very simple question to you. Is it still contested by the Defence that Fatmir Limaj at that point in time had the pseudonym Celiku?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, there's no contest because he gave evidence that he became known eventually by that name. The real question is at what point was he known --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: -- But he admitted that he was known eventually, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: So page 214, if you wouldn't mind just looking at that page, that's the question: Did Fatmir Limaj hold a position of command and control over the KLA soldiers? Now, this is why we said earlier on the context for all of this has to be those earlier sections, long sections, about the development of the KLA and its overall infancy during this period of time. Now, there are a number of witnesses, too many to really go through, but the two that the Prosecution were relying on are at page 215. They've already been mentioned more than once. They were both treated as hostile. I've indicated that the -- the Trial Court's position over these witnesses was an utterly recognisable and understandable one, because at the end of the day, may I say, let's take one of them as an example but it applies to both to a limited extent: Shukri Buja, paragraph 577. I can summarize the position. Before trial, as the Prosecution are now suggesting, exactly as they did at trial, all these issues were canvassed at trial there's nothing new that has been put before you today, that what he'd said in interview was, in fact, to be relied upon. Well, they discuss at paragraph 580, the difficulty of relying on a prior interview and so on. 581: "For these reasons the Chamber is not able to accept the truth of the evidence of Shukri Buja given in court as to the time frame at which Fatmir Limaj first assumed a position of command of a zone or area that included the prison camp ... that is the only evidence on this subject to which the witness purports to adhere. He has expressly disavowed in the relevant respects," and so on. It's saying there, "While the Chamber has strong suspicions" - in other words, why he has changed - "it is not able to make positive findings in favour of the Prosecution on the basis of what Shukri Buja said in the relevant parts of his expressly disavowed earlier statement." What they're really doing is, we say, a perfectly proper exercise of saying once you've got a witness who it appears is giving substantially different versions and it's possible that one of the versions is a lie, putting it straightforwardly on this issue, then the credibility of earlier versions also has to be looked at very carefully. No one's rewarding anybody; in fact, what's happening here is that Shukri Buja, as a whole, is being regarded with great care and it's the next paragraph which the Prosecution almost -- well, they mention it in passing, 582, but it's a very important paragraph, if you're going to -- I suggest you should not engage in reviewing the whole transcript or videos or whatever because we say there isn't an error of law here in approach or in actual evaluation. "The Chamber would also observe that, were it able to be satisfied to the truth and honesty of the relevant parts of what Shukri Buja said in the earlier statement, which is not the case, there remain some further difficulties in accepting from this that Fatmir Limaj had command of an area or zone which included Lapusnik ... at the time relevant to the Indictment." Now, this next section is extremely important because essentially the Defence at trial were suggesting that the process of interview was, we've put it in our brief, a form of spoon-feeding of these witnesses. And if you wish to be taken through it, you can see it on the video. "The manner of his questioning on that earlier occasion appears to have influenced important answers. Some answers, which can be understood as expressing a caveat were not followed up in the questioning to make clear what was intended. At one point, Shukri Buja describes Fatmir Limaj's role as one of coordination, a function he spontaneously equated with his own role ... Elsewhere the role is described as consultative. These references leave unclear whether Fatmir Limaj had a command role in the relevant sense. Further, there are passages which leave unresolved whether Fatmir Limaj or Ismet Jashari, a.k.a. Kumanova, was the person with ultimate responsibility for Klecka." And they mentioned further factors in relation to demeanour and Behluli on the succeeding pages, that's 226 and so forth. So I don't take you through each of these witnesses but merely point out that when one gets closer to the end, one begins to see not only is the context one of confusion and difficulty as to who was in charge of what zones, if you turn to paragraph 596, reference is there made to another Prosecution witness called Selimi. He was appointed commander of the 1st Operational Zone Drenica at the end of May. You'll see the dates. The first zone was Drenica, and in fact on one of the maps produced by the Prosecution at trial Drenica Zone did, in fact, include Lapusnik. It may be wrong but it means that it was never very clear. Sylejman Selimi testified that in this capacity he was responsible for organising the various units which were then acting in a more or less independent fashion. On his evidence, the Drenica Zone was to the north of the main road to Pristina but included Lapusnik. "It would appear from his overall evidence, however, that this refers to the part of the village to the north of the road rather than the southern part where the prison camp was located and that the main road through Lapusnik was the actual boundary of the zone." Now, it's the next sentence: "A significant aspect of Selimi's oral evidence is that from May to July," that's the indictment period, "there was not a single command, or commander, over the Celiku units, rather, the units were fighting independently from each other." That is precisely and was Fatmir Limaj's essential position. He had a unit at Klecka, he didn't have command of a unit, although he went to Lapusnik on a number of occasions over the three-month period he admitted that, but not to the camp. And that account, paragraph 597 is confirmed by Krasniqi - he is on the General Staff, he was a spokesperson, you may have noticed reference to him elsewhere - who testified at the relevant time there was no overall commander in the area which was to become Pastrik. So that if Lapusnik wasn't in Drenica to the north then the next zone to the south is Pastrik. But that doesn't become, as it were, formed until later. And the -- he is dealing with no overall commander in that Pastrik Zone and then he deals with Jashari being appointed in July. So one again sees how when one gets to the Defence witnesses, there's Fatmir and Ismet, and Shala and himself, all dealing with the same points and supporting, and it's 599. All the evidence that was being called was being supported and you will see 599 is a synopsis of Defence evidence on this. Now, these witnesses may not have been subjected to the same process because these witnesses were not shown to have been given earlier statements which were totally different, which applied to some of the Prosecution witnesses, but you will see tucked away in there, Zyrapi. "Bislim Zyrapi" - 599 - "further testified that his understanding was that Ymer Alushani," otherwise known as "Voglushi" -- now there's references, if I can just insert them here. You will find references to this commander at paragraphs 546 - I don't go back to them - 705 and 712 was in charge of Lapusnik, not Fatmir Limaj. So once again, you will see it's not a straightforward case and we say the Trial Chamber was perfectly entitled to come to the conclusions which they do finally on this page if I can just, I'll finish on this. They've examined other evidence, but their main conclusion is 601. "For the reasons identified in the preceding paragraphs" -- So they have given the reasons. They haven't just said, oh, well, there's a combination and that's it. They've given the reasons why they can't. "The Chamber is not able to be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt the Prosecution has established, in the period from May to the 26th of July" that he held a position of command. Then just skipping down a few lines: "That is so whether each relevant piece of evidence is considered separately, or in combination. As has been indicated even though there's a strong possibility" - so it's at one end of the spectrum to which they're entitled to come, and just because it doesn't satisfy the Prosecution assessment, doesn't mean to say that it's one that should be disturbed, unless it can be shown that it's wholly erroneous and we say that they haven't shown that - "that Fatmir Limaj was active as a commander in the prison camp at times relevant to the Indictment." And that is, in fact, the end of the judgement as it relates to Fatmir Limaj. The only other matter, perhaps, just in the final minute, we have put in answers to the questions, and in terms of the third question and JCE, I don't think there's any difference between our position and the Prosecution on that. And in relation to rogue elements we've given you hopefully all the references that you need to have in terms of weight, picked it up in the transcript. Unless there's any other question, I'm sorry I've rushed a little bit, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: No, it's not the case. I thank you, Mr. Mansfield, for your submissions on behalf of Mr. Limaj. We break now. We can resume at quarter to 3.00, 1445, for the response of Mr. Bala. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.53 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. We resume the hearing, and I will give the floor to the Defence of Mr. Bala for their submissions in response. You have the floor, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. It is a well-recognised principle in all jurisdictions, I believe, that the Prosecutor's duty is to seek justice, not merely to convict. I think a corollary to that would be with regard to some of the issues that I will be addressing this afternoon that a Prosecutor's duty is to recognise, especially where as here there has been careful consideration by the Trial Chamber, both as a finder of fact as well as one who has followed the law and articulated the following of the law, that such findings should not be disturbed. With regard specifically to the issue that has been raised by the -- question 3, I share in the comments made by my colleague beforehand, which was that we were in agreement with the Prosecution. And I also join in the submission that was made in terms of the facts being presented with regard to question number 2. I have no comment with regard to question number 3; it is outside of my bailiwick. And with regard to the issue of the Prosecution's appeal as it related to the joint criminal enterprise, I rely on the submissions that were made in the response to the brief, the written submissions, which takes me to the issue of sentencing. If this Chamber is to intervene with regard to the sentence that was imposed on Mr. Bala, the Prosecution must establish that the Trial Chamber committed discernible error, that no reasonable Trial Chamber could have imposed the sentence that was imposed in the case of Mr. Bala. If, and only if, it's demonstrated that the Trial Chamber committed an error in exercising its discretion, and one of the unique functions, obviously, of sentencing is the individualised discretion that is exercised by a Trial Chamber when looking at all the facts and circumstances concerning a particular defendant, or has failed to follow the applicable law, then and only then, will the Appeals Chamber substitute its sentence for that of the Trial Chamber. The record is really quite clear in this regard, and looking at the discussion in the judgement starting at paragraphs 722 and continuing through to 736, it is quite clear that the Trial Chamber made a careful and reasoned analysis of the factors that were to be taken into account in sentencing Mr. Bala. Not only did they in that regard take a look at the fact that he was not in a position of command, that he was a mere attendant, that he was following orders, that he had not obtained any perverse or particular pleasure from that which was done, but they also made a determination that he did not have any authority over the other KLA members. This is paragraph 726. And to the extent there is disagreement by the Prosecution that too much weight was attributed or not enough weight was attributed to those factors considered by the Trial Chamber, that complaint is not sufficient for the sentence imposed to be disturbed. I am pleased to note that today the Prosecution stated - this is at page 33 - and it was perhaps in a slightly different context but I think that the intent remains the same: "We do not seek in this appeal to go behind the Trial Chamber's remark about these witnesses in paragraph 26 and 28, insofar as requiring that they be corroborated on material particulars." To the extent that there is any reliance on L-96 for the purpose of suggesting that Mr. Bala's sentence should be enhanced in any way whatsoever, which was something that was asserted in pleading but I assume is no longer being asserted today, it certainly wasn't mentioned, that that is no longer part and parcel of what will be considered. One of the things that happened here, and although yesterday, I voiced clearly disagreement with some of the conclusions that were raised by the Trial Chamber, but one of the things that has happened here when examining the case, from the standpoint of sentencing is that the Trial Chamber, after considering all of the evidence, after considering all of the facts, the appropriate standards to be applied, made a determination that Mr. Bala was guilty of some and not guilty of other counts. And in that regard, at the conclusion of the trial, the Prosecution argued and in their brief they argued then, that the Prosecution submitted that accused Haradin Bala, if convicted on all counts, should receive a sentence of imprisonment of 18 years." He has not been convicted of all counts, said the Trial Chamber, paragraph 722. And based upon that reality, coupled with an assessment of the crime, the seriousness of the crime, and Mr. Bala's status, both in terms of his familial and life status as well as his involvement, which they found was that he should receive a sentence of 13 years. Based upon those considerations and no others, I think that at this juncture we would submit such a sentence fully meets the concerns and conditions of sentencing: Deterrence, retribution. He remains - and I say this with no rancor at all - he remains the sole individual to have been convicted, he had no leadership role whatsoever, and he will, if the Appeals Chamber maintains the sentence that he has at this time, suffer a period of conviction and incarceration which is substantial for an individual in his position. I'm not at this point going to argue some other compelling factors that may well exist for him because I don't think it is at this particular time an appropriate discussion with regard to an analysis of what the Trial Chamber did. And in that manner, I suggest that their reasoning and analysis was an appropriate one and one which should not be disturbed. There are some things that perhaps would be, shall we say, going over discussions of yesterday and that I choose not to do. Having discussed the issue of sentencing, at this point the submissions on behalf of Haradin Bala are concluded. And I trust that he will be treated appropriately by the Appeals Chamber in accordance with the law of the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Are there any questions from the Bench? That's not the case. Then I will turn to counsel for Mr. Musliu, Mr. Topolski, and give him the floor for his submissions in response. You have the floor, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. May I indicate on behalf of Isak Musliu that the submissions we shall make will be under five headings. First of all, will be some remarks by way of introduction; secondly, the approach of the Trial Chamber; thirdly, some submissions regarding the approach of this Chamber; fourthly, submissions regarding the three grounds of appeal; and fifthly, some final submissions. So may I begin with these remarks by way of introduction. On the 87th day of this trial I began my closing speech with a quotation. If that quotation was appropriate then, it is, in our submission, even more appropriate now. It comes from the opening lines of the closing speech of Associate Justice Robert Jackson to the international military tribunal in Nuremberg in July 1945 and he said this, and I quote: "An advocate can be confronted with few more formidable tasks than to select his closing arguments where there is a great disparity between his appropriate time and his available material." There is here much we could say, but we know our time is limited. This was the first trial arising directly and solely out of the conflict in Kosovo, and the first to see Kosovar Albanians on trial before this Tribunal. In opening our case, we suggested that the conduct of the KLA and the role of Isak Musliu within it could only properly be viewed against the prevailing conditions. We asked the Trial Chamber to give all proper and appropriate weight to the political and to the historical background. We asked them further to do something we suggest they did, indeed, do and to focus their consideration of the evidence on four matters: The extent to which, if at all, evidence presented by current or former members of the FRY forces and the MUP was or may have been tainted or influenced by bias or worse; the extent to which, if at all, those who made direct allegations of criminal conduct gave evidence directly or indirectly influenced to do so by others; the extent to which, if at all, there was any collusion -- I'm told you're having trouble hearing me. I've never been told that before. The interpreters are having trouble. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I have no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: The fourth matter we invited the Trial Chamber to give consideration to was the extent to which, if at all, given the nature of the locale in which these events occurred, there was or may have been, as we put it then, old scores or old feuds being settled. What followed, as Your Honours know, was a trial lasting some seven months in which the Trial Chamber saw and heard some 46 witnesses, to say nothing of the evidence received under the 92 bis procedure, and of course all the documentary material submitted by way of exhibit. The judgement was some five months in the making, running to nearly 800 paragraphs over 312 pages. The stature, the experience, and the standing of the three Trial Judges presided over by His Honour Judge Parker, who just 13 days before this judgement was filed became the Vice-President of this Tribunal, cannot be overstated nor overlooked. And so it is that of that constitution and of their judgement the following eight things have submitted by the Office of the Prosecutor. That it misapplied the standard of proof; that it entertained doubts not based on logic and common sense; that it failed to consider relevant evidence; that it erroneously evaluated the evidence it did consider; that it allowed itself to draw unreasonable inferences; that it took an erroneously piecemeal approach to evaluating evidence leading it to make wholly unreasonable findings of fact; that it erred in law, not only by failing to understand and apply the burden of proof, but also erred in law by failing to find the existence of a JCE which was, to the Office of the Prosecutor at least, "manifestly evident." All of that, in the submission of the Prosecution, led this Trial Chamber to reach factual conclusions that no reasonable Chamber could have reached; namely, in the case of Isak Musliu, three: That Musliu did not personally participate in the operation of a prison camp; that Musliu did not hold a position of command over KLA soldiers in that camp; and that Musliu was not, as a member of a JCE, individually responsible for all the crimes committed. That is all I say by way of introduction. Can I turn to the second heading. The Trial Chamber's approach to its task. Mr. Mansfield has already dealt with this, this morning. I seek to amplify and not to repeat his submissions. Under the heading we find in the judgement: "Considerations regarding the evaluation of evidence," in 25 paragraphs this Trial Chamber sets out its approach. It sets out its approach to various aspects of the exercise it was then to engage itself upon. In paragraph 10, on the burden and standard of proof, and please forgive me for forensically repeating myself, or rather, Mr. Mansfield. It is worth remembering this Trial Chamber in paragraph 10 said this: "Accordingly, the Chamber has determined in respect of each of the counts charged against each of the accused whether it is satisfied beyond reasonable doubt on the basis of the whole of the evidence, that every element of that crime and the forms of liability charged in the indictment has been established." Not entitled, said the Prosecution to morning, to apply that standard to each piece of evidence. Well, I leave that proposition hanging in the air for this Chamber to consider. In paragraph 12, it deals with the passage of time as a factor in considering testimony. In paragraph 13, on pre-existing loyalties as a factor bearing upon testimony. In paragraph 14, on the problems of how to approach and how to assess prior inconsistent statements. In paragraphs 16 to 20 on the issue central to the case of Isak Musliu, the proper approach to the question of identification evidence. It's worth interrupting myself and pausing to mention something that doesn't feature in the Prosecution's arguments. The spectre of mistaken identification hung ghost-like over this trial in the shape of Agim Murtezi, the man alleged to be the guard Murrizi. This is how I dealt with it in my closing speech, I referred the Chamber then to paragraph 157 of the Prosecutor's final brief when they said this: "The victims have a strong interest in ensuring that the correct individuals and not simply those on trial are held responsible, and therefore it is expected that some, if not all of the victims who testified, would have alerted the Tribunal in court if the wrong persons were on trial." That was a breath-taking submission in the light of the evidence, that the wrong man was put in the dock in this building and not one single Prosecution witness who admitted in cross-examination, seeing that man standing there, took any step whatsoever to play their part in putting right something that had gone wrong. That is why I say the ghost of mistaken identification hung over this trial. Can I return to the Trial Chamber's evaluation. At paragraph 26 it deals with the vitally important witness L-96. In paragraph 26, Dragan Jasovic, a man whose name has not yet featured before Your Honours, a man I suggested was a butcher. Dealt with in paragraph 27, he was the officer of the Serb police who first saw L-96 after he came out of Lapusnik and it was he who took L-96 to Lapusnik to begin this investigation, and on we go. In paragraph 28, the Trial Chamber sets out its position in relation to another vital witness in the case of Musliu, L-64. Again, it's worth interrupting oneself to mention this, that in its brief at 3 -- paragraph 3.32, and in its reply at paragraph 3.26, the Office of the Prosecutor submits to you that L-96 and L-64 are capable and should be regarded as being mutually corroborative. It seems from this morning's submissions that is not the position they maintain. Had they not said what they said this morning, what I would have said about it is that that is a brave submission to make in the light of the findings of the Trial Chamber in relation to L-96 and L-64. And, Your Honours, make no mistake. L-96 was at the heart of their case when Mr. Cayley opened this case, what feels like, to many of us, half a lifetime ago now, he said of L-96 he is the reason why we are all here. What did this Trial Chamber find about these two individuals? I'll just dip into the judgement for four short one-liners. Of L-96, they had a general distrust of him. Of L-96, they had "significant reservations" about his general credibility; paragraph 309. Of L-64, they found him unpersuasive, 321. "... reservations regarding reliability of substantial parts of his testimony." 324. "... extremely negative view of the credibility of this witness," paragraph 28. These two witnesses are at the heart of the case against Isak Musliu. That is all on the Trial Chamber's approach. Heading 3: Your approach. In our brief at paragraphs 10 to 16 inclusive, we set out our submissions there. It may be in due course of some assistance to this Court to consider the approach the Prosecution itself has sought to urge upon other constitutions of this Court when it has found itself responding to appeals in public filings. We have tried to gather together under four separate headings, as it were, the jurisprudence, and I don't place anything before you but I simply would wish to indicate, if I may, briefly the areas that we say may be of interest. And again, they've already been touched upon in some of the submissions that Mr. Mansfield made this morning and indeed in one or two of the questions Your Honours were good enough to ask of counsel, also this morning. The first is deference to the Trial Chamber as a Chamber -- as a trier of fact. In Oric, in a public filing in that case, Madam Prosecutor submitted this, and it's just two and a half lines, may I quote it: "An appellant cannot simply re-argue the weight of the evidence and invite the Appeals Chamber to resolve conflicts in his favour. Those tasks rest primarily with the Trial Chamber." In Krnojelac there are also articulations by the Prosecution in its public filings in that case which stresses, if it needs to be stressed, the proposition that this Chamber does not operate as a second Trial Chamber. The second heading of the jurisprudence can perhaps conveniently be placed under the title of its only unreasonable Trial Chamber findings that are overturned. Again, one doesn't have to develop it beyond, if I may say so without any attempt at sycophancy what His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen had to say in Tadic citing Brierly, and perhaps even echoing our Lord Helstrom [phoen], as many years before: "Different minds, equally competent," he said, "may, and often do, arrive at different results. Two reasonable persons can perfectly reasonably come to opposite conclusions on the same set of facts without forfeiting the title to be regarded as reasonable." Not every reasonable exercise of judgement is right, not every mistaken exercise of judgement is unreasonable." The third heading of the jurisprudence that will be familiar is, of course, assessing the evidence as a whole. We've already touched upon that. And finally, and again I think Mr. Mansfield read from it this morning, the Rutaganda Appeals Chamber holding on the difficult task faced by a Prosecutor in an appeal. So with that approach in mind, that approach to be adopted in mind, may I turn to the grounds of appeal in relation to Musliu. Ground 1: Personal participation in the camp. Trenchant criticism is made by the Prosecution of what it describes as the Trial Chamber's illogical piecemeal approach, which also failed along the way to consider all of the evidence. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber posed itself this question at page 269 of the judgement: "Was Isak Musliu identified at the Lapusnik camp?"
