Over the next 17 paragraphs and seven and a half pages, it, in our submission, closely, not to say, meticulously, analysed the evidence. It considered the evidence of witnesses such as L-04, L-06, L-10, L-12, L-96, L-64, and Ruzhdi Karpuzi. This is the only bit of detail I even want to touch upon, let alone get into, for we say briefly it can speak volumes. L-04 implicated Qerqiz in the murders of two victims. He also claimed that Qerqiz beat him, L-04. He claimed that he'd learnt Qerqiz's real name was Isak Musliu. Who did he learn that from? He learnt it from one (redacted). Who was (redacted)? (redacted) was a villager living close to Mr. Musliu. (redacted) made a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. (redacted) was a Prosecution witness but they didn't call him. The Chamber was unreasonable, in the submission of the Prosecution, to consider that there was no basis for this co-detainee's identification of Musliu. They submit in their brief at 3.55, another submission that in our respectful view borders on the breath-taking. They say that the basis for the co-detainee's identification was unambiguously before the Trial Chamber. Unambiguously refers to the absent (redacted) who was called to give no evidence, and so the Trial Chamber's conclusion that there was no reliable basis by that route for a finding that Qerqiz was Musliu is characterised by this Prosecution as being unreasonable. It's worth noting that L-04 in his first two statements to UNMIK made no mention of Qerqiz. L-10, and this cross-refers if Your Honours want to look at it in due course at judgement paragraphs 330 and 331, claim that Qerqiz had beaten him and had possibly been involved in the murder of Fehmi Xhema otherwise known as Fehmi Tafa. In relation to that murder, L-06 gave a completely different account. He made no mention of any Qerqiz and said that it was Ramadan Behluli and Ali Gashi who were responsible for that death. L-10's evidence in relation to beatings by Qerqiz was contradicted by the evidence of L-06. He said he was not able to distinguish Qerqiz from other soldiers in the camp. L-12 claimed he was beaten by someone called Rrahman Qerqizi. He didn't know who Rrahman Qerqizi was and he didn't identify Isak Musliu. Forgive us dipping into the detail, but the devil lies in it, we submit, because faced with that combination of evidence or lack of it, it is said by the Prosecution, as we understand them, that it was not reasonable for this Tribunal -- Trial Chamber to come to the decisions it did. Your Honours, before I go on may I make it absolutely clear that the answer to Judge Pocar's question 1 submitted to us kindly on the 30th of May, 2007, is: Yes. Should I just remind everybody what the question was. "Do the Prosecution and the Defence for Musliu agree that it is undisputed that Isak Musliu's pseudonym in the indictment was Qerqiz?" It is. Sometimes I cross-examine witnesses by beginning by saying, I represent Qerqiz; no issue. Prosecution suggests that the Trial Chamber failed to consider the relevance of that pseudonym --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. -- Judge Meron wants to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, on this question of Qerqiz, if I may pursue that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is there any evidence in the trial record to suggest that any individual other than Musliu might have had this name, Qerqiz, nickname?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, with the one exception I suppose of what I just submitted to you regarding L-12, saying he was beaten by someone called Rrahman Qerqizi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So this is as close you come to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: That's as close as I get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I never suggested, never part of my case, that there was another Qerqiz who could be culpable, never part of my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Just to keep the record straight, is it now your submission that Qerqiz was, indeed, a pseudonym for Mr. Musliu?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It's undisputed --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: From that agreed fact may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then -- because counsel Powles mentioned at transcript 5586: "Either by that name, Isak Musliu, or by his nom de guerre, Qerqiz, which of course is a shortened version of Qerqiz Topulli, a famous Albanian national hero."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Of course, not an issue. The issue of course is whether it's Isak Musliu. The Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you explain what you meant by the last comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Can I simply take you to reference as to how we put it. In our -- in our respondent's brief at paragraph 54, just for Your Honours' cross-reference, we say this that: "There was evidence before the Trial Chamber to establish that Isak Musliu was known as Qerqiz. That does not mean that such evidence was available to witnesses to assist them in establishing that the masked man they claim was Qerqiz was, in fact, Musliu." It is inconceivable that this Trial Chamber did not weigh that simple concession in the balance. They knew, for they said so many times, that Musliu and Qerqiz were synonymous. For example, at paragraph 694 of the judgement they refer to Qerqiz -- Musliu, a.k.a., Qerqiz. At paragraph 712, likewise, they describe him in the same way. And therefore, that is why we submit it is inconceivable that the Court did not take that into account. The point was plainly before them. It did not, to their satisfaction, establish beyond reasonable doubt that the masked man claimed to be Qerqiz was, in fact, Isak Musliu. And I hope that, for His Honour Judge Meron's benefit explains rather more bluntly the slightly elliptical way that I put it before. I hope that makes it clear. Your Honours, against the background of caution with regard to identification evidence that is well-known, we submit that the Trial Chamber carefully and fairly analysed the evidence and reached a clear conclusion, and the clear conclusion it reached in paragraph 716 was, and I quote, that: "It was unable to conclude that Isak Musliu had been reliably identified as the person described in this evidence." They reached the clear and unequivocal conclusion that the only witness to have purported to have identified Musliu was L-96, and the less said about him, the better. Can I move on to ground 2 and Musliu's command position -- Your Honours, I look at the time. I notice in scheduling I was split into two lots of 30 minutes. I don't know whether Your Honours want me to stop now or finish. I will finish in the next 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I would prefer that you finish your submissions in the total time of one hour allotted to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I then go on to deal with ground 2. Musliu's command position. The issue at trial was simple. It was conceded that Musliu held a position of command. It was the Prosecution's case that he held the position of command over the soldiers in the prison. Again, the Trial Chamber posed for itself precisely the correct question, judgement, page 276 -- paragraph 276, question: "Did Musliu hold a position of command and control over the soldiers in the camp?" It then proceeded to answer its own question under three headings, may I just give them to you for reference purposes. First of all, under the heading: "Celiku 3 unit," judgement paragraph 277. Secondly, question: Were there other units operating in Lapusnik?" Judgement paragraph 280. And thirdly: "Was Isak Musliu commander of Celiku 3 or the overall commander of the Lapusnik area?" 281. There is no complaint that I have read nor heard from the Prosecution as to that approach, that is to say, no one is suggesting the Tribunal is asking itself the wrong or inappropriate questions; their submission seems to be they reached the wrong answers. Over 22 paragraphs, the Trial Chamber analyses in answering those three questions the evidence of no less than 11 witnesses by my count, including Fatmir Limaj himself and others, including Shukri Buja and Ruzhdi Karpuzi, the last two of course were found to be hostile. As far as Karpuzi is concerned, may we just make this submission, because the Prosecutor puts it at the heart, Ms. Brady, of her careful submissions this morning, that this is extremely important. Suggestion seems to be this, that Karpuzi may have also seen and not just heard Isak Musliu singing, and that somehow makes sure what was hitherto doubtful. That seems to be the position the Prosecution take. We simply submit this: To so submit, is to give that evidence a value it neither holds nor deserves. There was no issue that he heard him singing, probably no issue, considering I put the question: Did you see and hear him? Saw him and heard him singing. It adds nothing, we submit, and in any event if I'm wrong about that it was still before the Trial Chamber, they still considered it, and took it no further. So it is that, we suggest, that in a careful and, again, measured analysis of this issue, the Trial Chamber considered all appropriate aspects and features, posed for itself the correct questions, and reached a clear conclusion founded upon evidence it could feel sure about. And if that isn't in short form a proper and appropriate exposition of the task of any finder of fact in a criminal jurisdiction, I don't know what is, with respect. Can I turn then to ground 3 and JCE. May I adopt, respectfully, Mr. Mansfield's submissions and adopt Mr. Guy-Smith's adoption of them as well. The Trial Chamber analysed and summarized the position regarding committing offences through participation in a JCE. There seems to be no criticism of that analysis, no criticism of that approach. The focus of the complaint seems to be upon paragraphs 665 to 669 in the judgement, in that the Trial Chamber, it is said, erred in requiring that individuals be specifically identified and erred in not finding that the crimes fell within the scope of a JCE. May I indicate what our responses are to that. As the Prosecution failed to prove participation in a JCE by planning, by ordering, by instigating, by committing, or by aiding and abetting the crimes charged, as they failed to prove liability via 7(3), then even if a JCE existed, there was no basis upon which the Prosecution could contend that Musliu was a party to it. That much was consistently our position and remains so. It can be looked at and seen in our final brief at paragraph 1039. That's a position we took then and maintain now. Furthermore, we submit, that the Trial Chamber plainly understood and properly applied the legal principles engaged. In applying those principles, it carefully placed them against both the reality and the evidence. And so I come to my last heading, some final remarks. Your Honours, whether in the case of the appeal of Isak Musliu it was justifiably and appropriately brought will perhaps be for this Chamber to say. Whether the submissions made by the Prosecution in this appeal sit comfortably alongside the position it has taken in other appeals, to say nothing of the position it has taken in the appeal of Mr. Bala, will also be perhaps for this Chamber to say. But what can be said with some confidence is that the case of Musliu stands alone in the history of this Tribunal. He is the first, and as we understand it, the only case on which a wholly acquitted defendant called no live evidence on his behalf, gave none and called none. Through us, he put the Prosecution to proof of its case. That evidence spoke over 85 days culminating in a detailed and reasoned judgement. For this appeal to succeed, this Chamber would have to be satisfied of either an error of law invalidating the decision or an error of fact which has occasioned a miscarriage of justice. We simply submit that neither has happened here. The position we took at trial presented a stern test for the Trial Chamber whether it would fearlessly, fairly and justly apply the burden and standard of proof. We submit it did so. The Prosecution, in effect, say to you, Your Honours, We don't agree with the answers it came up with, therefore they were being unreasonable. Indeed, an extraordinary challenge has been made in the case of Isak Musliu today by this Prosecution. Your Honours, no respect -- disrespect is, of course, intended and none, we are sure, will be taken due to the fact that Isak Musliu has chosen not to attend this hearing. As at trial, with the utmost respect to the Court, he leaves the decision to you through us. What should that decision be? That this appeal should fail. Your Honours, that's all I propose to say unless I can be of any assistance in answering any of the Court's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, am I right from the record in understanding that the person called Qerqiz always appeared masked?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: During all the events relevant to the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. With one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: With one exception regarding Witness L-64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Which only pertained to entering and exiting together.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But there is no -- no one saw him unmasked during any of the relevant events in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I do confirm that -- well, I suppose with the exception of L-96 who purports to recognise him from the past, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But not in the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well -- yes, L-96 said he saw Musliu in the camp and Musliu was someone he knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: But our criticisms of L-96 and the Court's view of him, of course is well known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other question? Well, if it is not the case, this concludes the response on behalf of Mr. Musliu. I will give the floor to the Prosecution for their reply for up to 30 minutes. That's the agreement we had this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I begin, I would like to answer the question that Judge Schomburg asked the Prosecution before the break. I wasn't able to give a very detailed response to the question about Witness Karpuzi and the effect of -- the potential effect of him being a hostile witness. And I've had the opportunity to do some further research into this issue over the break. What I can inform the Chamber of on Karpuzi is this: The witness was declared hostile to the Prosecution on the basis that there were material differences between his oral evidence and his prior statements. Now, those differences did, in fact, relate, there were three differences, and they all related to the case against Limaj; such as, the role Limaj played in an oath ceremony. They did not relate specifically to Mr. Musliu. Now, Karpuzi was declared hostile, a hostile witness, for the Prosecution on the 8th of February, 2005, and again after that declaration of hostility, most of the cross-examination, the main thrust of that, referred to Limaj and nothing we could call crucial in relation to Musliu. All of the evidence that Karpuzi gave concerning his sighting of Musliu in the oda in the main house in the -- the singing occasions, all of that evidence had already been in evidence prior to the declaration of him as hostile to the Prosecution. Now, as to the question of the use of his prior statement, I mentioned and it's still our position, that unlike the case of Prosecution witnesses Buja and Behluli, who were declared hostile, and there was a decision relating to those two to allow in their evidence as substantive evidence. That's not the case in relation to the statement of Karpuzi; however, his statement, which is P136, was -- was given this exhibit number, P136, and the Prosecution was enabled or allowed to cross-examine the witness on this prior statement. Now, you've asked, that's the prelude to your question, you've asked what's the effect of him being declared a hostile witness. We couldn't find any discussion of this particular issue in our quick researches over the break. The -- we have to say we're not sure that the motive for his hostility to the Prosecution, in fact, extended to Musliu, given what I've just set out about how -- the manner in which he was declared hostile. However, if the motivation for his hostility to the Prosecution did extend to Musliu, then our submission on it would be this: In fact, a hostile witness should be given in many ways more weight in his in-court testimony. The hostility is an expression of motive or bias in the testimony of a witness, and so his testimony has to be evaluated in that light. Explains why a witness says things in order to protect an accused. And it also, in our submission, could give more weight to the incriminating matters, the incriminating things, that the witness says about a particular accused. I also would make the submission that this particular matter, whether he saw Musliu singing on occasions in the oda, to this witness could have seen quite insignificant. So even if he was trying to protect Musliu, as it were, this witness may not have realised the significance of saying such a thing. And that in itself provides a very valuable probative force to his evidence in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Now, if I may, in the time remaining, I'll try to reply as briefly as I can to both the responses of Mr. Mansfield for Limaj and Mr. Topolski for Mr. Musliu. I'll speak first about some general points, some common points to both of their responses. I'll try to do it in a structured way speaking immediately after Mr. Topolski. In some respects I will be a little bit more fulsome in what I say to Mr. Mansfield's responses, that means no respect to -- no disrespect to Mr. Topolski's submissions but in many respects, they are shared. The first point made by Mr. Mansfield and joined in by Mr. Topolski is that, essentially, what we really object to as the Prosecution are the Trial Chamber's factual findings because there's no fault in the Trial Chamber's legal approach and both Mr. Mansfield and Mr. Topolski reminded this Chamber of the various paragraphs, they took us through the various paragraphs in the judgement, to show that the Trial Chamber articulated correctly the standard of proof, it knew what that was, and it knew -- it set out correctly how -- the manner and how to evaluate evidence. And Mr. Mansfield even referred to our own statement we made in the reply that -- to the same effect the Trial Chamber does correctly articulate the standard of proof in the manner of its application. And they submit, in essence I think it was summed up, crystallised by Mr. Mansfield, when he said it actually beggars belief that the Trial Chamber did not employ the methods it set out. This, on its face, is a superficially attractive argument but in our submission it is not borne out upon a proper review of the judgement. We too have read, as Your Honours have, all the references. For example, in paragraph 10, where the Trial Chamber finds it has to be satisfied on the whole of the evidence. But the very point of our appeal, and I think we've made this point throughout our brief and this morning, is that a proper review of the judgement and the forensic analysis contained in it shows this slip, this chasm between the statement of principle set out in the judgement and how, in fact, the Trial Chamber applied it. As a subpoint, both Mr. Mansfield and Mr. Topolski made a submission to the effect that by our very bringing of this appeal, by the Prosecution bringing this appeal, that somehow we're impugning the integrity of the Judges, that we're not taking into account the calibre of the Judges and their experience. We want to stress that our appeal has nothing to do with the Judges in their personal capacity; that goes without saying. Our appeal is in relation to their capacity, their function, as triers of fact in this case. We obviously accept their calibre; that's not the issue. And in this respect we would also point out that this Chamber has dealt with several trial judgements in the past where the Trial Chamber has misapplied the standard of proof to one set of facts or made a factual error in one part of the judgement and not in other parts. And we've seen this Chamber correct a number of trial judgements on that basis, both when appeals are brought by the Prosecution as well as when they are brought by the Defence. The next point that Mr. Mansfield made is that -- and, again, it's a general point, that we're just merely relitigating the case, that we want the Appeals Chamber to basically step in the shoes of being a second Trial Chamber and to hear the matter de novo. Well, in some respects, it's true. We do object to the Trial Chamber's factual findings, but it's not as they would put it just because we don't like them. It's because they're ones that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached on the evidence, and we fully endorse the comments of the ICTR Appeals Chamber in the Rutaganda appeals judgement, there's no issue with that and we also agree that the Prosecution has a heavy burden of persuasion when it appeals against acquittals. Again, we take no issue with that. But in our submission this was a wholly erroneous decision, even bearing in mind this array or spectrum of outcomes that Mr. Mansfield spoke of. And most importantly, this is not just a factual appeal, it's a factual appeal framed by legal error. Our appeal is more than just there were errors of fact; our appeal is that these errors came about by the Trial Chamber's legally erroneous approach to the evidence and the application of the standard of proof. So it is, as it were, a factual appeal in a legal jacket. The next point that Mr. Mansfield made is to the effect that the suggested remedy that we have argued for is totally unworkable or, as he put it, totally impractical. And largely because this Chamber would have substitute and make its own credibility and reliability assessment in place of a Chamber which heard all the live witnesses. I said it before this morning so I can be very brief on this, we concede that the remedy situation, the remedy here is difficult because the effect of the legal error is so far-reaching and the affected factual findings are so numerous. However, the Chamber does have the power to revise Trial Chamber decisions; this is in Article 25, and indeed has entered convictions before, I mentioned the case of Tadic, also the case of Krnojelac and Rutaganda. It's revised sentences before in the case of Galic. And in any event, it accords with the standards of review that this Chamber has set out in the Blaskic and Kordic decisions. I also mention that practically speaking there was a way in which the Appeals Chamber could place itself as in that same box seat of the Trial Chamber, and that is that the transcripts and the videotapes of this entire trial remain and can be watched. I also suggested, however, that there was another possible remedy and that was to remand the matter for a new trial, and that would of course preserve parties' right to appeal. Now, there's a submission he made, I hope I understood him correctly, this is Mr. Mansfield. He made a submission to the effect that the Trial Chamber did not itself suggest that it was applying the standard of proof to predicate facts --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters. He made the submission that the Trial Chamber did not suggest that it was applying the standard to predicate facts but that it was reserving it for ultimate issues. And then if I understood him correctly, he indicated that this would be -- the standard should be applied to each witness, that the Trial Chamber was correct to say for each witness to the effect, Can I be sure about this witness? That was the import of his submission. Well, on this point the Prosecution does depart from the Defence's position. The standard is not to be applied to each witness or each individual item of evidence; therein lay the error. And in cases of this nature, I'm talking firstly about complex circumstantial cases, but also in a wider sense of war crimes cases being prosecuted many years after the events with all the well-known difficulties in evidence collection. There's rarely a smoking gun, as it were, there's rarely one piece of evidence which is the piece de resistance upon which a conviction rises or falls, and that is the reason why a Trial Chamber must be extremely careful to apply the beyond-reasonable-doubt standard at the correct stage and not to each witness and each document in the expectation that that will be -- that witness or that document will be sufficient or the answer. On his specific points relating to the case of Mr. Limaj, I'll only respond to a few points made by Mr. Mansfield. Basically, the first point he made was that the Trial Chamber's summary of the accounts of the six witnesses was accurate and they did a very careful job at looking at their reliability closely, and he mentioned that the Court factored in for Ivan and Vojko Bakrac that they were possibly influenced by the television images they saw. This submission is not sustainable, in our submission. Both Ivan and Vojko Bakrac can pinpoint where and when -- when and where they first recognised the commander from the camp. Ivan Bakrac recognised him first on the television, then on the internet. Vojko Bakrac said it was when he was watching television in the main house. And we can well imagine that that recognition is something that would stick in their mind and there's no question arising for those two, at least, that they could have later been influenced by media images, which brings me to the phenomenon of unconscious transfer and Mr. Mansfield said that this is a very subtle -- this can be a very subtle phenomenon and that the problem is that when you get someone as -- someone who gets as much attention as Limaj later got, that a witness can retrospectively later think that it was the person, that the person was there. We note -- in reply -- in reply, we submit that Wagenaar's evidence was actually not to this effect. His evidence was to the point that if someone sees someone that they do not know, then is exposed to media images, and then asked to identify, that's not a reliable identification procedure because of that potential for unconscious transfer. Nowhere in his evidence, nowhere in his evidence, did he say that when a person sees media images of someone and recognises the person then and there on that image, that that would be similarly tainted as an unreliable identification. And if I could give Your Honours an example, it would be as if today I meet somebody for the first time, I converse with them. Next week, I'm watching the news and I see that person on television and I recognise that person. I think, Oh, that's the person I met last week after the hearing. Even if I then later became exposed to media images of that person, it is difficult - this is a common-sense point of view - it is difficult to see how that could then create a retrospective memory that when I saw the news item in the first place, I recognised him. Mr. Mansfield also pointed out the various reservations the Trial Chamber had with each witness, and in particular paragraphs 560 and 561 dealing with individual and combined effects of this evidence. I think we've dealt with this at length in our appeal brief and this morning, and I don't need to say anything further on that. On the position -- Mr. Limaj's position of command, he highlighted the Trial Chamber's findings in the early part of the judgement which show that the KLA was in some kind of evolving or embryonic, I think he said, or fluid state, and he argued that this was somehow inconsistent with our position that Limaj was in command. In our submission, it's clear from these early findings of the Trial Chamber, it's clear that the KLA was going through some kind of evolution. Zones were developing at different rates, but there's nothing inconsistent with those findings, and our position that the evidence leads to only one reasonable conclusion, that even in this period, June/July, one bright line emerged; Limaj emerged as the intermediary level of command over units in this area. Now, brigades and battalions may not have been officially created until, you know, August, but that doesn't mean that they were not operating as such earlier, and that's our point. And in any event, we note that there was clearly enough organisation of these units for the Trial Chamber to be satisfied that Article 3 could apply and -- to these crimes and all the requisite organisation that that article requires. Turning to the position of the Trial Chamber to Mr. Buja and Mr. Behluli's prior interviews. Mr. Mansfield argued that it was completely understandable, the Trial Chamber's position, because - I'm summarizing his position but - for him it's when a witness essentially does a U-turn, does an about-face on his earlier version, it's quite -- if I can -- excuse me, if I start that submission again. He argued that when faced with a witness who does an about-face on his earlier version so that the Trial Chamber finds that that in-court evidence is a lie, then the credibility of his earlier version has to be looked at carefully. That might well be the case, but what the Trial Chamber did was effectively to render void its earlier decision to allow in the earlier statements, allowing them in for their substantive truth. We set out the matter in detail in our briefs, but essentially the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 581 and 586 initially reject -- reject the earlier statement without reason. The -- the language of the judgement, if I take Your Honours to paragraph 581 as an example, the last line of 581, last couple of lines, the Trial Chamber notes: "He has expressly disavowed in the relevant respects what he said earlier when interviewed. While the Chamber has strong suspicions in all the circumstances it is not able to make positive findings in favour of the Prosecution on the basis of what Shukri Buja said in the relevant parts of his expressly disavowed earlier statements." And a similar thing is said about Mr. Behluli's earlier evidence in paragraph 586. Now, we of course realise that there were additional reasons set out in the later paragraphs as to why, even if they were going to give it weight, they couldn't. But in our submission if you review those interviews you will see that these additional reasons simply are not borne out by a review of those interviews, and especially -- it would not justify outright rejection of the earlier statements, the whole statement going out for these very particular reasons, especially those parts of the statements which were corroborated. I'll turn now to Mr. Musliu's -- brief reply in relation to Mr. Musliu. I've already mentioned many common points. In relation to Witness L-64 and L-96, yes, the Prosecution -- we are not going behind the position that L-64 and L-96 require corroboration, and to be clear, we are not suggesting or we do not now suggest that they -- that the Trial Chamber was wrong to find that these two witnesses could not corroborate each other. However, the additional element now is that Witness Karpuzi, had the Trial Chamber not made its error relating to Witness Karpuzi, that this witness now provides the corroboration for both. Mr. Topolski also made the submission that to the effect that our case at trial more or less rose or fell on L-64 and L-96, we don't agree with that. Our case at trial was always a case based on the entirety of evidence, including L-96 and L-64, but all the witnesses, all the witnesses who spoke of being beaten by a masked man who was referred to as Qerqiz, and the other evidence regarding proximity and command. On his individual criticisms of the various witnesses, L-04, L-10, and L-12, I won't -- everything that I need to say is in our briefs and I won't go further than that, except to point out once again that it's not each individual item of evidence that's important; it's the combination and the strands of evidence which the Trial Chamber was wrong not to draw together to find that Isak Musliu was, indeed, the beater known as Qerqiz, the masked man in the camp. On the question -- on what flows from the confirmation that his name is -- his pseudonym during the time was Qerqiz, the important point is, of course, that the witnesses, the three witnesses, heard that name as they were being beaten or seeing others being beaten. And we don't agree that we would have to prove that there was no other Qerqiz possibly in the area, but we agree we would have to disprove that there was a reasonable possibility that these references were not to him but to someone else. However, in our submission, there was no evidence suggesting there was another one in the area and there was no witness or document which even suggested it and that the strength of the evidence flowing from the various strands of evidence proved this -- made this the only reasonable conclusion, that Qerqiz, the man referred to as Qerqiz, was Isak Musliu. He made a submission that -- about Mr. Karpuzi's evidence and the relevance of this particular piece of evidence. However, he -- Mr. Topolski did not deal with the two main points, not only is the Karpuzi evidence -- as a result of the error the Trial Chamber made, that Karpuzi's evidence was not only that he saw Musliu in the oda, but it was on occasions, and there's also a certain familiarity that stems from those occasions, a familiarity that the Celiku 3 unit, the soldiers of that unit, had with the camp as expressed by Karpuzi, in his evidence attesting to witnessing and being part of these singing get-togethers in the oda, this access that the Celiku 3 soldiers had to the main house in the camp. And finally he did not deal with the point, the main point about Witness Karpuzi that we spoke about, that he corroborates both of L-64 and 96 regarding his presence in the camp. Likewise, Your Honours, Mr. Topolski did not -- he spent -- in terms of the error relating to Musliu's command, his submissions were directed towards the error, the second error, as to whether or not he was the effective commander, the effective commander. However, he did not properly answer our -- the first error, and that is that on the Trial Chamber's own logic, the own logic of its findings, that is, that it was an organised KLA-run camp, that there was no other unit south of the road but Celiku 3, and that he was an effective commander and if -- together with all the evidence that Bala and other guards were from that unit, there is no other reasonable conclusion but that he had effective command over the prison. I'll stop here. I don't know how we're doing for time. I may discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You have just one minute to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. BRADY
utterances.text: Okay. I will finish my submissions here and ask Your Honours to uphold the Prosecution's appeal against both Isak Musliu and Fatmir Limaj. My colleague Mr. Wirth may wish to make use of that last one minute remaining to make a brief comment about joint criminal enterprise. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Just very shortly. I will quickly reply to the Defence's written submission on the Trial Chamber's second question whether there was evidence regarding opportunistic visitors. The Defence referred to the following pieces of evidence, Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen's evidence. Now, the important thing about Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen's evidence is that Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen at the time did not know that the camp existed, therefore her evidence cannot possibly relate to the camp. Second, Jan Kickert's evidence, and I would also like to note that the Trial Chamber only relied on Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen's evidence and there is a good reason for that namely that all the other evidence that has been put before us is either irrelevant or exclusively and explicitly based upon speculation. Mr. Kickert's evidence is irrelevant. Mr. Kickert spoke of break-away KLA factions in western Kosovo. Well, Lapusnik is not in western Kosovo, it is in central Kosovo and there certainly was no suggestion that a break-away KLA faction was in the Lapusnik camp. Jakup Krasniqi's evidence. Jakup Krasniqi's evidence was basically -- sorry, he was asked that if any bad things had happened, would he not agree that they could only have been committed by rogues and Mr. Krasniqi agreed to that. He gave no evidence about the actual existence of rogue elements. And finally, Shukri Buja's evidence. Shukri Buja noted a number of times that he had no recollection of any concrete acts of individual revenge and he too merely agreed to a hypothetical possibility. Now, I'd like to conclude with a note that Mr. Buja's lack of knowledge regarding the acts of personal revenge is particularly relevant here because Mr. Buja actually knew the camp. On occasion, he escorted persons who were released from the camp to their home, and as I mentioned this morning he was involved in getting a person released from the camp. Therefore, in sum, the Trial Chamber was correct in not relying on the evidence that I just referred to, and obviously it also shouldn't have relied on Ms. Ringgaard Pedersen's evidence. Thank you. That concludes the submissions of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you for your submissions. This -- there are no questions, I believe. So this concludes the submissions of the parties in this appeal. In the Scheduling Order we had scheduled a brief personal address by the -- by Mr. Limaj, Mr. Bala, and Mr. Musliu, but I note -- I noted yesterday Mr. Limaj and Mr. Musliu decided not to exercise their right to be present. So I understand they, of course, waived their right to address the -- personally the Court. As to Mr. Bala, equally, I understand that by being absent this afternoon and by consenting that the appeal hearing proceeded in his absence, he waived the right to address personally the Court today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would concur with the comments you've made. I believe that he had -- some things were a bit more pressing at the moment on his mind. And I, once again, do apologise for his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I appreciate that. Well, this brings us to the end of this appeal. Before concluding the hearing, I would like to thank counsel for the Prosecution and the Defence for their submissions and cooperation with the Court. I would like also to thank the Tribunal's personnel that assisted in the conduct of the hearing, and of course the interpreters for making the dialogue between the parties possible. The appeals judgement will be rendered in due course. The Appeals Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.14 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24
